10.7-2 Section 206AA v. DTAA

There was a controversy whether section 206AA applies to non-residents or not, in terms of the provisions of DTAA. The provisions of section 90(2) of the Act prescribes that provisions of the Act are applicable to the extent that they are more beneficial to the assessee and since section 206AA prescribes higher rate of withholding tax, it would not be beneficial to the assessee and therefore, the rates prescribed in DTAA can prevail.

Earlier, CBDT had clarified vide Press Release [No. 402/92/2006-MC (04 of 2010), dated 20-1-2010] that section 206AA will also apply to all non-residents in respect of payments/remittances liable to TDS which reads as under:

"A new provision relating to tax deduction at source (TDS) under the Income-tax Act, 1961 will become applicable with effect from 1st April, 2010. Tax at higher of the prescribed rate or 20 per cent will be deducted on all transactions liable to TDS, where the Permanent Account Number (PAN) of the deductee is not available. The law will also apply to all non-residents in respect of payments/remittances liable to TDS" (Emphasis supplied)

The Bangalore Tribunal in case of Bosch Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 141 ITD 38 held that the provisions of section 206AA clearly override the other provisions of the Act. Therefore, a non-recipient whose income is chargeable to tax in India has to obtain PAN and provide the same to the assessee deductor.

However, recently the Tribunal in following cases held that in case of non-resident, even in absence of PAN, the TDS can be deducted as per the rates prescribed in DTAA.

Dy. DIT v. Serum Institute of India Ltd. [2015] 68 SOT 254 (Pune)

In terms of the decision of Supreme Court1 as well as CBDT Circular2 , the provisions of DTAA override provisions of the Act, if contrary to the provisions in DTAA. The amendment and the Rule, which may be prescribed, may be examined on the basis of the above legal position.

8.5-4 What if stamp duty value is revised up-wards by state govt. between the date of Agreement To Sell (ATS) and date of sale deed/registry?

Agreement to sell fixes the consideration for the property deal. There might be a gap of 3 months or even more between date of ATS and sale deed. During this time, the circle rate may be re-vised upwards. However, the sale consideration will not be revised upwards. It is the amount agreed in ATS which will change hands.

To avoid hardship in genuine cases, the first proviso to section 50C(1) provides that stamp duty value on the agreement to sell shall be taken as full value of consideration. The second proviso to section 50C(1) provides that the first proviso shall apply only where consideration or part thereof has been received by way of an account payee cheque or account payee DD or by use of Electronic Clearing System (ECS) through a bank account or through pre-scribed electronic modes on or before the date of ATS. In terms of Rule 6ABBA, the prescribed electronic modes of accepting payment are (a) credit card, (b) Debit card, (c) Net Banking, (d) Immediate Payment Service (IMPS), (e) UPI (Unified Payment Interface), (f) RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement), (g) NEFT (National Elec-tronic Funds Transfer) and (h) BHIM (Bharat Interface for Money). The second proviso condition has been imposed so that people don't make back dated Agreement to Sell showing re-ceipt of cash to avail the lower circle rate.

Here, a word of caution needs to be sounded. The cash component of the entire deal should be less than Rs. 20,000 and bal-ance should be received by seller by way of account payee cheque or account payee DD or by (ECS or prescribed electronic modes of payment). If the seller accepts Rs. 20,000 or more in cash, it would re-sult in violation of provisions of section 269SS and attract penalty under section 271D.

Sub-section (1F) is inserted to provide that sale of motor vehicle of the value exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs will also require collection of tax at source at 1% (see para 10.8-2);

It has made the consequential amendment in the definition of 'buyer' under Explanation (aa) to include purchaser of a motor vehicle and 'seller' under Explanation (c) so as to include an individual and HUF being the service provider (see para 10.8-5).

10.8-2 Sale of Motor Vehicle [Sub-section (1F)]

In terms of the amendment, if the value of motor vehicle exceeds Rs. 10,00,000, the seller will collect tax @ 1% of the value of such motor vehicle at the time of receipt of such amount from the buyer.

The transaction may be in cash or by the issue of a cheque or draft or by any other mode.

10.8-2a "Motor Vehicle" - Connotation of - 'Motor vehicle' has not been defined specifically under the Act. However, it is defined under section 2(28) of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 which reads as under :

'"motor vehicle" or "vehicle" means any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads whether the power of propulsion is transmitted thereto from an external or internal source and includes a chassis to which a body has not been attached and a trailer; but does not include a vehicle running upon fixed rails or a vehicle of a special type adapted for use only in a factory or in any other enclosed premises or a vehicle having less than four wheels fitted with engine capacity of not exceeding thirty five cubic centimetres."'

The above definition is only for the purpose of Motor Vehicle Act. Therefore, such meaning cannot be extended to the Income-tax law. Even Supreme Court in case of Assistant Commissioner (Anti-Evasion-I) v. Swaraj Mazda Ltd. [2001] 121 STC 255 held that in absence of the definition of the words 'motor vehicles' in the Sales-tax Act, the meaning given to 'motor vehicles' in the Motor Vehicle Act cannot be given to the said expression occurring in the Sales-tax Act or in the Notification issued thereunder.

20.4-6 Procedure in case of Loss of C form The dealer should only submit one copy (marked as 'Original') to seller. If it is lost, he can send original copy marked as 'Duplicate', unless the State Rules required submission of Original copy only. [Even the 'duplicate copy' of the form is printed and supplied by department itself. It bears the same serial number as the original form. Hence, it is 'original' duplicate copy. It is not duplicate of original copy].

If buyer sends both copies marked 'Original' and 'Duplicate' to seller and if both are lost, then following procedure should be followed.

If duly completed or blank C form is lost when it was in custody of purchasing dealer or when the form was in transit to selling dealer, the purchasing dealer will have to furnish 'Indemnity Bond' to sales tax authority (from whom the blank forms were obtained) in prescribed 'G' form. If the duly completed C form is lost after it is received by selling dealer, he has to submit indemnity bond to sales tax authority of his State.

Duplicate C Form - If C form is lost, the purchasing dealer can issue duplicate declaration in 'C' form with clear declaration in red ink that this is a duplicate declaration being submitted. Details of earlier certificate number (which was lost) and of selling dealer has to be given. [This will be necessary if both original copies of form i.e. 'Original' and 'Duplicate' are lost].

It may be noted that there is no provision to submit certified Xerox copy of earlier certificate and Xerox copy is not acceptable - J N Jetiwa v. State of Maharashtra - (1995) 11 MTJ 491 (Mah Trib). Only duplicate copy can be issued by purchasing dealer to selling dealer. In Delhi Automobiles P Ltd. v. CST (1997) 104 STC 75 (SC), submission of photostat of 'C' form was held as not permissible even when buyer company was under liquidation and photostat was issued under order of High Court judge under whom the buyer company was under liquidation.

20.4-7 Selling dealer not liable for false declaration by buyer

The seller has to be satisfied that the purchaser is a registered dealer and that the goods purchased were specified in the certificate of registration issued to the buyer. For this, he can rely on the representation made by the buyer (purchasing dealer) in the C form. If the purchasing dealer misapplies the goods, the penalty can be imposed on the purchaser, but selling dealer, who has relied on C form issued to him by the buyer, cannot be held liable - State of Madras v. Radio and Electricals Ltd. - (1966) Supp SCR 198 = 18 STC 222 (SC) - followed in State of Orissa v. Bharat Petroleum (2001) 122 STC 559 (Ori HC DB) * State of AP v. Askin Fabs (1999) 112 STC 550 (AP HC DB) - same view in Polestar Electronic v. ACST AIR 1978 SC 897 = 41 STC 409 (SC) - followed in Dy CST v. Bharat Refineries (1978) 41 STC 409 (Ker HC) * MRF Ltd. v. ACST (2000) 117 STC 23 (Ker HC DB) * Karthik Electric Controls v. CTO (2008) 15 VST 450 (Mad HC DB) * Essar Oil v. Intelligence Officer (2011) 37 VST 192 (Ker HC DB).

Purchasing dealer is entitled to rely upon the certificate of registration of selling dealer and to act upon it. He is entitled to concessions even if registration certificate of selling dealer is cancelled with retrospective effect - State of Maharashtra v. Suresh Trading Co. (1998) 109 STC 439 (SC) - same view in Chunni Lal v. CST (1986) 62 STC 112 (SC).

Even if CST Registration certificate is cancelled with retrospective effect, the C forms issued earlier would be valid. The C forms cannot be cancelled with retrospective effect - Jain Manufacturing v. Commissioner (2016) 93 VST 326 (Del HC DB).

Selling dealer is not required to hold an enquiry with regard to purpose for which the materials have been purchased by purchasing dealer. Once he furnishes necessary declaration forms from purchasing dealer, nothing more is required to be done. - K G Industries v. STO (1999) 113 STC 49 (MP HC) - same view in Tej Pratap Shukla v. Relevant date for valuation of unexplained gold bars

3.2

Whether section 269ST relieves person receiving payment from complying with TCS/section 13A etc.?

A question arises whether section 269ST is in addition to obligations under other provisions? Or applicability of section 269ST would preclude applicability of obligations relating to TCS, obligations under section 13A in regard to receipt of cash donations by political parties etc.?

Consequential to the insertion of new section 269ST, the Finance Act, 2017 has omitted section 206(1D) which obligated the seller to collect TCS @1% if cash component of sale consideration exceeded Rs. 5,00,000 in case of sale of jewellery and Rs. 2,00,000 in case of sale of other goods/services. Thus, where it is intended that applicability of section 269ST would preclude application of other provisions, the Finance Act, 2017 has specifically provided for the same by omitting sub-section (1D) of the section 206C. Further, proviso to section 269ST provides that the restriction on cash payments in section 269ST shall not apply to :

(i)

Government,

(ii)

any banking company, post office savings bank or co-operative bank,

(iii)

in respect of transactions of the nature referred to in section 269SS; and

(iv)

such other persons or class of persons or receipts, as may be specified by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette.

In view of the above, unless the Central Government expressly exempts cash receipts covered under other provisions or obligations, it has to be presumed that applicability of section 269ST would be without prejudice to other provisions applicable to cash transactions.

- Section 206C, prior to amendment by Finance Act, 2016, provided that the seller shall collect tax at source at specified rate from the buyer at the time of sale of specified items such as alcoholic liquor for human consumption, tender leaves, mineral being coal or lignite or iron ore etc. It also provided for collection of tax at source at the rate of one per cent on sale in cash of bullion exceeding 2 lakh rupees and jewellery exceeding 5 lakh rupees. In order to reduce the cash transactions in sale of goods and services. Finance Act, 2016 has expanded the scope of section 206C(1D) (omitted by the Finance Act, 2017, w.e.f. 1-4-2017) to provide that the seller shall collect tax at the rate of one per cent from the purchaser on sale in cash of any goods (other than bullion and jewellery) or providing of any services (other than payment on which tax is deducted at source under Chapter XVII-B) exceeding two lakh rupees. So far as sale of Jewellery and bullion is concerned, the provisions of sub-section (1D) of section 206C prior to its amendment by the Finance Act, 2016 shall continue to apply. Further, with a view to bring high value transactions within the tax net, it has been provided in sub-section (1F) of section 206C (as it stood prior to 1-1-2025) of the Act that the seller who receives consideration for sale of a motor vehicle exceeding ten lakh rupees, shall collect one per cent of the sale consideration as tax from the buyer. Any person who obtains in any sale, the goods of the nature specified in sub-section (1D) or (1F) of section 206C is a buyer. The seller for the purposes of collection of tax under section 206C shall be—

(i)

A Central Government or a State Government.

(ii)

Any local authority, or corporation or authority established under any Central, State or Provincial Act.

(iii)

Any company, firm or co-operative society.

(iv)

An individual or Hindu undivided family who is liable to audit as per provisions of section 44AB during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which the goods are sold or the services are provided.

The amendments brought in section 206C by Finance Act, 2016 are applicable from 1st June 2016.

In this regard a number of queries have been received about the scope of the provisions and the procedure to be followed. The board has considered the same and decided to clarify the points raised by issue of a circular in the form of questions and answers as follows:

Question 1: Whether tax collection at source ('TCS') at the rate of 1% is on sale of Motor Vehicle at retail level or also on sale of motor vehicles by manufacturers to dealers/distributors.

Answer: To bring high value transactions within the tax net, section 206C of the Act has been amended to provide that the seller shall collect the tax at the rate of one per cent from the purchaser on sale of motor vehicle of the value exceeding ten lakh rupees. This is brought to cover all transactions of retail sales and accordingly it will not apply on sale of motor vehicles by manufacturers to dealers/distributors.

Question 2: Whether TCS at the rate of 1% is on sale of Motor Vehicle is applicable only to Luxury Cars?

Answer: No. As per sub-section (1F) of section 206C of the Act the seller shall collect the tax at the rate of one per cent from the purchaser on sale of any motor vehicle of the value exceeding ten lakh rupees.

Question 3: Whether TCS at the rate of 1% is applicable in the case of sale to Government Departments, Embassies, Consulates and United Nation Institutions for sale of motor vehicle or any other goods or provision of services?

Answer: Government, institutions notified under United Nations (Privileges and Immunities) Act, 1947, and Embassies, Consulates, High Commission, Legation, Commission and trade representation of a foreign State and shall not be liable to levy of TCS at the rate of 1% under sub-sections (1D) and (1F) of section 206C of the Act.

Question 4: Whether TCS is applicable on each sale of motor vehicle or on aggregate value of sale during the year?

Answer: Tax is to be collected at source at the rate of 1% on sale consideration of a motor vehicle exceeding ten lakh rupees. It is applicable to each sale and not to aggregate value of sale made during the year. This can be explained by way of an illustration:

Illustration: Motor vehicle worth 20 lakh is sold and for which payments are made in instalments, one at the time of booking and the other at the time of delivery. At the time of booking 5 lakh rupees are paid and 15 lakh rupees are paid at the time of delivery. Tax at the rate of 1% on 5 lakh rupees at the time of booking and at the rate of 1% on remaining 15 lakh rupees at the time of delivery shall be collected at source.

In the result, capital gain tax would be chargeable in assessment year 2009-10 and not in assessment year 2010-11. I have sold my residential house in Delhi for Rs. 3 crores and the resultant long-term capital gains is Rs. 1.95 crores. The agreement for sale was entered into with the buyer on 15.01.2019 and advance amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was received from buyer by cheque. With the help of the advance amount, new house was purchased in Delhi for Rs. 1.5 crores on 01.03.2019. Balance amount of Rs. 1.5 crores was received on 29.03.2019 and registry in buyer's name was effected and possession was handed over to him on that date. Investment made in another flat in Haryana of Rs. 50 lakhs on 30.03.2019. Will my capital gains be tax-free on the basis of the amended section 54?

The benefits for once-in-life-time exemption of long-term capital gains upto Rs. 2 crores from transfer of residential house based on investment in 2 houses in India is applicable with effect from assessment year 2020-21. In other words, transfer of residential house should be made on or after 01.04.2019. Date of transfer is date of possession to buyer or date of registry whichever is earlier. Here, possession and sale deed registry done in buyer's name prior to 01.04.2019. Therefore, the benefit under the amended provisions of section 54 shall not apply. In the result, assessee will be able to claim deduction in respect of investment in any one house only…obviously he will claim in respect of Rs. 1.5 cr. house. The balance long-term capital gains of Rs. 45 lakhs shall be taxable.

What if in above example, the sale deed in buyer's name is executed and registered on 02.04.2019 and possession handed over to him on that date?

In this case, the entire capital gains on Rs. 1.95 crores shall be tax exempt as cost of investment in two residential houses in India exceeds Rs. 1.95 crores and both these houses have been purchased within a period of one year before the date of transfer of old house.

What if capital gains from transfer of old residential house is Rs. 2.5 crores and seller invests Rs. 2 cr in 2 residential houses in India and balance Rs. 50 lakhs in specified bonds under section 54EC?

Here, the capital gains arising from sale of old residential house exceeds the limit of Rs. 2 crores. Hence, assessee will get deduction of Rs. 50,00,000 under section 54EC. He will also be able to deduct cost of one of the two new houses in India bought by him (the one whose cost is higher). The balance long-term capital gains shall be taxable. The limit of Rs. 2 cr. is with reference to capital gains arising from transfer of old house and not with reference to capital gains chargeable to tax.

Whether relief will be available in old residential house abroad is sold and resultant long-term capital gains not exceeding Rs. 2 crores is invested in 2 houses in India?

Yes. Section 54 is applicable regardless of where the old residential house is situated. Only that resultant capital gains must be invested in 2 houses in India.

Would the tax benefit be lost if total cost of both the houses in India in which capital gain is invested exceeds Rs. 2 cr?

The Rs. 2 cr. limit is with reference to capital gains arising from transfer of both houses and not with reference to investment made. In fact, investment should be equal or should exceed the amount of capital gains to avail section 54 benefit.

Resultant long-term capital gains from sale of old house is Rs. 1.5 cr. The total investment in both houses in India is Rs. 1.3 crores. Can the balance capital gains of Rs. 20 lakhs be invested in section 54EC bonds to avail deduction under that section?

Yes. If after making investment in both houses still some capital gains not exceeding Rs. 50 lakhs remain, the same can be invested in section 54EC bonds to avail deduction under that section. Availing the two-house benefit is no bar to availing deduction under other sections.

It is clear that (i) above lays down the principle for determination of FMV while (ii) and (iii) lay down the documentation that needs to be used to support the FMV.

Point (ii) above is not happily worded. 'In case the jewellery is received by the way of purchase on the valuation date' would literally mean where someone purchases jewellery he would be taxed on the invoice value of the jewellery. If someone purchases jewellery at its FMV, then nothing is taxable under section 56(2)(x)(c)(A)/(B). This is not the intention of the provisions. What this means is the donor purchases the jewellery from registered dealer with proper invoice and makes a gift on the same day to any person, then point (ii) above will apply and FMV will be the invoice value. Point (iii) would apply to cases other than point (ii) which includes a situation where jewellery is purchased by donor on one date (say 1-4-2017) and gifted to donee on another date (i.e. 2-4-2017).

Point (iii) also is confusingly worded when it says 'In case the jewellery is received by any other mode and the value of the jewellery exceeds rupees fifty thousand, then assessee may obtain the report of registered valuer'. The wordings seem to suggest that it is optional for the assessee to obtain a report of registered valuer as regards FMV in these circumstances. So, it would appear that assessee may use the report of registered valuer or any other evidence to substantiate the FMV. If the assessee does not obtain any valuation report nor produces other evidence, the Assessing Officer will have recourse to section 142A(1).

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

HEADNOTE: Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained money -  Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessees were dealers in diamonds - Each of assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 - Said declaration was accepted by Department and a certificate was issued to respective assessees under VDIS, 1997 - During relevant assessment year, assessees sold jewellery declared under VDIS, 1997 and offered to tax capital gains arising from respective sales - Assessing Officer disallowed assessees’ claim holding that sales transactions were not genuine - Tribunal, however, allowed assessees’ claim - Whether since identity of purchasers had been established and amounts received from purchasers had also been accounted for, in absence of any material to contrary it was to be concluded that transactions were genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in allowing assessee’s claim - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees were dealers in diamonds. Each of the assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997. The said declarations were accepted by the Department and a certificate was issued to the respective assessees under the VDIS, 1997. The assessees claimed to have sold the jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 in the year relevant to the assessment year 1998-99 and offered to tax the capital gains arising from the respective sales. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessees on the ground that the persons to whom the jewellery was sold had stated in their statements that the transactions were not genuine and, although, later on the statements were retracted and affidavits were filed on oath to effect that the transactions were genuine, but the transactions were not proved. Challenging the aforesaid orders, appeals were filed and ultimately the Tribunal allowed the claim of the assessees and deleted the additions.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

In aforesaid circumstances, it was to be held that the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessees' claim. [Para 7]

The first and foremost reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject the explanation of the assessee is that persons from whom assessee claims to have been received advance are not responded to summons issued under section 131(1) and in few cases, they have denied any kind of transactions with the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not discharge its onus cast upon as per the provisions of section 68, in respect of cash receipts, and thus, opined that cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee from various persons is unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has committed a fundamental mistake in examining the cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee towards sale of jewellery in light of provisions of section 68. Be that as it may. The fact remains that, the assessee has furnished name and address of the customers from whom it has received cash for sale of jewellery. The assessee need not obtain confirmation and submit to the Assessing Officer, because, the law does not mandate collecting PAN details of the persons, if sale value of jewellery does not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs as per rule 114B of Income-tax Rules, 1962. In so far as compliance of KYC norms, it is mandatory under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with effect from 4-5-2023 onwards and not applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

[Para 10]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. It is stated by the assessee that there is no onus on the assessee under any law to reveal the identity of buyers who allegedly bought gold bars from the assessee, this argument is fallacious as the amount of cash allegedly received from unknown buyers of gold bars stood deposited in the bank account of the assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor.

Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act . That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further. In the instant case, the department had examined four persons, who had declared jewellery under the VDIS and effected sale of such jewellery to the assessee-firm. The Assessing Officer had examined the genuineness of the business of purchase and sale of jewellery carried out by the concerned jeweller. There are no fetters on such powers of the Assessing Officer. The department was not hampered or impinged, by the immunity outlined in the VDIS to undertake such investigations. Hence, there was no justification in the stand of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the acceptance of the VDIS declarations by the Department in the hands of the sellers of the jewellery to the assessee made the impugned investigations contrary to the letter and spirit of the VDIS. Another important feature, which according to the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the case of the assessee was the registration of the assessee under the Punjab General Sales-tax Act, 1948. The crux of the dispute revolved around the purchase and sale of old diamond jewellery, which had been made only up to the period 17-3-1998. After 17-3-1998 and upto 31-3-1998, no such purchase or sale had been effected. The sales made up to 17-3-1998 had not been made a subject-matter of the sales tax returns submitted by the assessee, as admitted by the assessee. It was being sought to be explained on the ground that such sales were within the period of exemption and, hence, no sales tax was exigible on such sales. Be that as it may, the fact remained that such sales had not been subject to any verification/examination by the sales tax authorities too, for the same, being sales up to 17-3-1998, had not been reported in the sales tax return filed by the assessee. The reference made by the Commissioner (Appeals) to the assessee's sales tax assessment order, dated 4-12-2000, was also misplaced because that was in relation to the subsequent period, which was not relevant to the assessment year under consideration. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) erred in relying on the assessment order of the sales tax authority, dated 4-12-2000, for the subsequent period and the surrendering of sales tax registration certificate on 11-3-1999 to repeal the inference of the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the inference of the Assessing Officer that no actual business of purchase and sale was carried out by the assessee was justified and deserved to be upheld.

HELD: The nature of business of the assessee is not disputed that he is engaged in the wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. It is also not in dispute that in this line of business sale of jewellery in cash is normal trade practice. T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14] In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

Assuming the revenue was right in its contention that the sale did not involve actual delivery of diamond jewellery, then unless it was established that the assessee had passed on his undisclosed income to T, it could not be said that the amount received by the assessee from T represented the undisclosed income of the assessee. Neither T in his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 had stated that the assessee had given the cash amount to T nor in the reassessment proceedings the Assessing Officer had gathered any evidence to that effect. Perusal of the reassessment order showed that the Assessing Officer had not made any efforts to link that the cash received and deposited by T in his bank account was, in fact, paid by the assessee. In those circumstances, in the absence of any cogent evidence brought on record, the decision of the Tribunal in holding that the Assessing Officer had failed to establish the nexus between the cash amount deposited in the bank account of T was attributable to the cheque issued by T in favour of the assessee could not be faulted. [Para 18]

In the instant case, cash credits were not introduced in the accounts of the assessee. From the fact that the cash credits were introduced in the accounts of T, it could not be inferred that the said cash belonged to the assessee. The assessee was not under any obligation to prove the cash credits in the accounts of 'T'. The assessee had proved that he was in possession of the diamond jewellery which was duly declared and certified under the VDIS, 1997. He had proved the identity of the person to whom the said diamond jewellery was sold, his creditworthiness and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from the sale of the diamond jewellery. [Para 19]

The sale transaction of diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 between the assessee and T had been accepted by the Sales Tax Authorities and the assessments made them had attained finality. In any event, in the facts of the instant case, the view taken by the Tribunal that the retracted statement of T was corroborated by the pay-in-slips/cash deposits in the bank account of T and the non-availability of the jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee to T was a reasonable and possible view. [Para 20]

Therefore, the appeal filed by the revenue was without any merit and was liable to be dismissed. [Para 21]

FACT: A search and survey action under section 133A was carried out on the premises of assessee-company, engaged in the business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery and bullion. It was noticed that the assessee had deposited huge amounts in its bank account after demonetization was announced.

During the course of survey, a statement of the company's MD was recorded wherein he stated that the amount deposited was received from 2153 customers on 8-11-2016 and each customer had paid an advance of less than 2 lakhs for purchase of bullions. Said bullions were to be purchased from ALG, owned by one NS. He thus filed a declaration of Rs. 40 crores under the PMGKY scheme, however, withdrew same later on.

Subsequently, the assessee filed its return admitting an income of Rs. 1.42 crores after adjustment of certain brought forward losses. The case was selected for scrutiny and certain statutory notices were issued on it.

The Assessing Officer completed assessment by making addition of Rs. 40.11 crores under section 68 and assessed the assessee's income at the rate of 60 per cent as per section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the additions made under section 68 to the extent of Rs. 28.37 crores on various ground; firstly, that the statement of third party given before police/E.D. was not contradicted by the AO; secondly, no inquiry was made from the parties whose details had been given by third party and thirdly, the deposit of cash by the third party in the account of the assessee has not been disputed by the Assessing Officer.

Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ In any given case, whether the sales claimed by the assessee are genuine or not, is a question of fact and the answer will depend on specific facts and circumstances of the case. In the present case, the addition has been made, disbelieving the assessee's claim that cash sales in SBNs were made, amounting to Rs. 9.25 crores on 8-11-2016. The case of revenue rests essentially on hypothesis that it was unlikely, based on materials available on record, surrounding circumstances, human conduct, preponderance of probabilities and nature of incriminating information/evidence available on record, that cash sales amounting to aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores were made in SBNs on 8-11-2016. No specific transaction of sale, not even one, has been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue. In fact the Assessing Officer himself has treated sale amounting to Rs. 75.99 lakhs (made in SBNs) to be genuine but has disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.25 crores. In the absence of any direct evidence to show that any specific sale transaction was not genuine or untrue, the question of fact before us is whether in the given facts and circumstances it is possible that the assessee might have made sale of aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores in cash on 8-11-2016. It is quite understandable, that after announcement of demonetization, the people in possession of SBNs were desperate to use it for purchase of gold, diamond and silver jewellery and other items before the deadline after which SBNs could not have been used. In such a desperate situation, it is quite understandable that customers would not exercise choice in selection as they might have done in normal course. Therefore, the submissions made from assessee's side that the customers instantly purchased whatever they saw on the counter, using SBNs, is acceptable. Further it is quite understandable that the assessee brought additional manpower to deal with and to attend to the extraordinary rush of customers. Therefore, the submission made from the assessee's side that family members, relatives, friends and staff of other business entities were utilized to attend the extraordinary rush of customers is also acceptable. It is not in dispute that the aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.25 crores included sale amounting to Rs. 1.67 crores which attracted penalty under section 271DA for contravention of section 269ST. Further it is not in dispute that the aforesaid total sales of Rs. 1.67 crores (consisting of each transaction exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs in cash) were not made through serially numbered sales vouchers. Instead, these transactions were interspersed with other sale transactions in cash, below Rs. 2 lakhs. These facts clearly establish that the sales claimed by the assessee to have been made in cash were genuine. Moreover, the contention that if the assessee had any intention to book bogus sales, then the assessee would not have booked sales inviting penalty under section 271BA is a reasonable one. It is further seen that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the assessee's books of account. Moreover, the assessee has shown the sales in VAT returns, which have been accepted by VAT authorities. It is not in dispute that the assessee had sufficient stock in trade to make sale as claimed, on 8-11-2016. Revenue has not doubted the purchases made by the assessee. Further not even a single specific sale transaction has been proved to be fake, bogus or untrue.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: ■ The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

Once the assessee has recorded sales in the books of account, which is supported by necessary sales bills with a corresponding stock-in-hand, the Assessing Officer ought not to have made additions towards cash deposits as unexplained money only on the ground that, there is abnormal variation in cash sales during the demonetization period when compared to earlier or subsequent periods. It was a well-known fact during the demonetization period that, there was a mad rush in jewellery shops for purchasing gold jewellery out of demonetized currency when the demonetization was announced on 8-11-2016. In the instant case, going by the facts available on record, the assessee has reported major sales on 7-11-2016, which is the previous day of the demonetization was announced, and from the details furnished by the assessee, it is very clear that, the assessee has made sales of gold jewellery in cash which is the source for cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period on 14-11-2016. Since the cash deposited into the bank account is supported by necessary cash balance available as per books of account maintained by the assessee which was further supported by necessary sales bills, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards cash deposits under section 69A as unexplained money cannot be sustained. Although the Assessing Officer has disbelieved the sales on the basis of VAT returns submitted by the assessee for the month of November, 2016 and claimed that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover backdated sales, but going by the history of the assessee in filing the VAT returns, it is evident that, for all the months in the financial year 2016-17, the assessee has filed VAT returns belatedly and from the above, it is very clear that, the argument of the Assessing Officer that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover up backdated sales, is contrary to the evidence available on record and cannot be accepted. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A. Thus, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made under section 69A. [Para 20]

During the year under consideration the assessee deposited Rs. 91,00,000/- in demonetized currency. The cash so deposited was accumulated cash which was received against for sales made in the proprietorship concerns of assessee by it over the period of the year prior to demonetization, majorly during the period from 28-10-16 and 29-10-16 and such sales was part of total sales credited in trading a/c. and the assessee has already offered income on such sales in Trading Account by reducing the cost of sales from sales. The Assessing Officer herself accepted the sales shown in trading a/c. and has not disturbed the cash sales so declared by the assessee and the sales of assessee duly supported by the sale bill and invoice and duly verifiable form books of account including stock register and considering availability of stock on hand, it proved that the sales made by the assessee are genuine sales recorded in the books of account. All the details required to prove the sales made by the assessee were provided in the assessment proceedings. The assessee has filed sufficient evidence to substantiate his sales. He has filed (1) Copy 56 Cash book and sales bills along with submission dated 10-12-2017 (2)Copy of stock register for the financial years 2015-16 and 2016-17 (which shows that before making the sale the sufficient stock was available with assessee (3) Copy of VAT Returns APB and VAT assessment order of proprietorship concern Dinanath Raj Kumar, Jaipur. The VAT department accepted the sale of the assessee. Thus the assessee substantiated its claim from the documentary evidence and also with the facts. In letter dated 6-6-2019 the assessee submitted to Assessing Officer that increase of cash sale in month of Oct. and Nov. 2016 was due to Karva Chouth, Dhanteras and Diwali sales (Festival Season). Further the assessee has explained the Assessing Officer that, the firm Dinanath Raj Kumar has been started in the year 2015 itself and during the financial year 2015-16 the mother of the assessee has expired and hence the assessee was not able to setup his business at Kanpur and hence the sale was low in the year financial year 2015-16 as compared to sales in 2016-17. The assessee is engaged in the business of Jewellery and gold. The higher cash sales on festival season Karva Chouth, Dhanteras and Diwali is general feature in the trade of the assessee and such sales is also apparent from the cash book submitted during the course of assessment proceedings. Looking to the above facts and circumstances of the case the sale made by the assessee is genuine which is executed after giving the goods to the customer, duly reflected in the invoice issued, assessee having sufficient stock in the books, sales is duly reflected in the books of account supported by payment of VAT and the revenue has not brought any positive material to prove it as bogus sales. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee did not have the sufficient stock for making the sales. Thus, it cannot be said that the figures of sales and purchases are not supported by the quantity details

Even those persons who responded to notice under section 133(6) could not substantiate the source of funds. Therefore, he rejected cash sales made during demonetisation period and taxed cash deposits under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]
