HEADNOTE: Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Sales during demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee was engaged in business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) - During demonetisation, assessee made cash sales of Rs. 10.28 crores on 08-11-2016 - Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to income of assessee under section 68 - It was noted that no specific transaction of sale, not even one, had been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue - Allegation of Revenue holding that cash sales of aforesaid amount claimed by assessee to be untrue, was without convincing materials - Aforesaid addition had been made by Revenue based merely on suspicion, doubt, conjecture and guess work - Assessee had provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.24 crores even after announcement of demonetisation - Moreover, assessee had shown sales in VAT returns, which had been accepted by VAT authorities - Whether, on facts, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Para E.2.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) and other items of gold, silver and diamond. The assessee made a total deposit of Rs. 10.28 crores in the bank out of cash sales made on 08-11-2016. The aforesaid cash deposits in bank were made out of Specified Bank Notes (SBN) in the denomination of 1000 and 500, which were demonetized with effect from 09-11-2016.

■

The Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to the income of the assessee under section 68.

■

The assessee's appeal was dismissed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading in bullion and jewellery. During demonetization, the assessee had deposited a significant amount of cash in its bank accounts. The assessee explained that the cash deposits were out of cash advances received from customers against cash sales of jewellery/bullion.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and treated the amount of cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68, read with section 115BBE, and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The entire case of the revenue is built upon the basis of suspicion regarding the sales booked by the assessee prior to the start of demonetization period. The Assessing Officer has rejected the books of account merely because there was a spike in cash advances on three dates. However, the comparative data furnished by the assessee clearly dispels this suspicion. A perusal of the chart reveals that the cash sales in the year under consideration were in fact significantly lower than the preceding year. When the assessee has demonstrated that in the previous year, during the corresponding period, the cash sales were much higher, the allegation of ‘abnormal’ sales during the demonetization period falls flat. The data furnished by the assessee shows that the assessee’s total sales as well as cash sales during the year under consideration including the relevant demonetization period were comparatively very less than the preceding financial year. This data shows that the assessee’s cash sales were not abnormal during the relevant period and Assessing Officer’s suspicion of cash sales is not based on any reliable material. [Para 11]

■

Further, the Assessing Officer has not pointed out any discrepancy in the stock register, and the assessee was evidently possessed of the requisite stock to effect the impugned sales. It is a matter of record that the purchases have been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income. The notices issued under section 133(6) were largely complied with, and the mere fact that one party went into bankruptcy does not make the entire purchases bogus. Though the Assessing Officer has doubted the purchases, it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had not debited the amount of purchases from its books or that the assessee had made purchases out of its unexplained income. Once the purchases are accepted and the stock is not disputed, the sales flowing out of such stock cannot be treated as non-genuine. The sales have been recorded in the books of account and the profit arising therefrom has been offered to tax. Therefore, the entire receipts from the corresponding sales cannot be treated as unaccounted income of the assessee; only the profit element embedded in such sales can be taxed, which the assessee has duly offered for taxation. Taxing the gross receipts again under section 68 would amount to double taxation of the same amount. [Para 12]

■

Even, at the most, it can be alleged, though not proved, by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had made certain sales and accepted SBN/demonetized currency during the relevant period. Even assuming so, the assessee may have breached or violated the relevant circular/notification of the RBI/Demonetization Scheme, however, even then it cannot be held a case of income from unexplained sources. [Para 14]

■

defect/discrepancy was found in the physical stock vis-a-vis book stock of the assessee. [Para 20]

If the allegation of the Assessing Officer is accepted that the assessee has inflated its sales during 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016, then there has to be some discrepancy in the book stock vis-a-vis physical stock, but no such discrepancy was found because no such sales were inflated by the assessee. [Para 21] Merely because there was a minor variation in the cash sales during the alleged period compared to previous year would not mean that the assessee has inflated its sales to cover up demonetized currency. [Para 22]

During the year under consideration, Diwali was on 31-10-2016 and it is common knowledge that in our society, festival runs 15 days after Diwali and it is also a common fact that once the demonization was declared by the Prime Minister, there was frenzy in the market and people were purchasing goods they never intended to purchase just to get rid of demonetized currency. [Para 23]

For the sake of repetition, the assessee had furnished month-wise purchases, month-wise details, stock register, valuation of closing stock, month wise details of cash sales, copies of VAT returns and not a single defect has been pointed out by the Assessing Officer in these clinching evidences. [Para 24]

The most important fact is that since the cash sales have already been offered as income, the same cannot be taxed in the garb of inflation sales to cover up demonetization currency. [Para 25]

In so far as the allegation of non-mentioning of names of the purchasers is concerned, it is not only baseless but without any backing of law as the assessee is not required to keep the names of purchasers for cash sales less than Rs. 2 lakhs and not even one instance has been pointed out by the Assessing Officer where cash sales were more than Rs. 2 lakhs. [Para 26]

Considering the vortex of evidences, there is no merit in the impugned addition made by the Assessing Officer and also in the part relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals). Therefore, considering the totality of facts, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to delete the impugned addition. [Para 27]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading in gold and jewellery - During demonetization, assessee had deposited substantial amount of cash in his bank accounts - Assessee claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers for gold scheme - Assessing Officer treated cash receipts as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to prove genuineness of credits found in his bank account - It was noted that assessee had filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there was no discrepancy in books of account - Further, assessee had reported sales made before date of demonetization to GST authorities - Whether since assessee received trade advances in cash and same had been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68 - Held, yes - Whether furthermore assessee had furnished name and address of customers from whom it had received cash for sale of jewellery and law did not mandate assessee to collect PAN details of persons, if sale value of jewellery did not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs, assessee had satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of persons and thus, additions under section 68 was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 13, 14 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading of gold  diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. - Assessing Officer on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three parties were bogus - Accordingly, he made an addition - It was observed that assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers - Further, information gathered by Investigation Wing was based upon statements of persons who were managing affairs of assessee’s suppliers, however, these witnesses were not subject to cross examination - Whether, on facts, said purchases could not be treated as bogus and, therefore, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 26] [In favour of assessee]

Sections 3D(1), (2), (7) , 4A of the U.P. Trade Tax Act, 1948 - Purchasing dealer not furnishing Form III-C to the selling dealer - Sales by the selling dealer shall be treated as sale to unregistered dealer - Section 3-D (1) is subject to Section 3-D (2) - Sale by new unit without Form III-C - To be treated as sale by new unit to the purchaser taxable in the hands of seller - No purchase tax can be levied on the purchaser - Who purchased the goods from new unit - Exempted from payment of tax.

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Cash deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was deriving income from business of jewellery in his proprietorship concern and interest income from saving bank account, FDR and parties - Assessing Officer noticed that assessee had deposited cash of certain sum in its bank account during demonetization period viz. between 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 out of which cash of certain sum was in demonetized currency notes (SBN i.e. Old Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes) - Assessee explained it to be out of cash sales made by him - Assessing Officer tried to analyze cash sale vis-à-vis cash sales in earlier years and had also observed that cash sale so shown during demonetization was exceptionally high vis-à-vis cash sale in financial year 2015-16 however, he also observed that total sales for entire year had decreased substantially in current financial year when compared with previous year - He further held that assessee had not provided name, address and PAN of customers to whom cash sales was made - Accordingly, Assessing Officer observed that these cash sales were not real sales and assessee had tried to introduce his own unaccounted money in garb of cash sales and therefore, made addition under section 68 - It was noted from records that increase of cash sale in month of Oct. and Nov. 2016 was due to Karva Chouth, Dhanteras and Diwali sales (Festival Season) - Further assessee had explained that, firm had been started in year 2015 itself and during financial year 2015-16 mother of assessee had expired and hence assessee was not able to setup his business at Kanpur and hence sale was low in financial year 2015-16 as compared to sales in 2016-17 - Whether looking to above facts and circumstances of case, it could be said that sale made by assessee was genuine and not bogus which was executed after giving goods to customer, duly reflected in books of account supported by payment of VAT - Held,yes - Whether further, since sales were below prescribed limit so it was not compulsory or mandatory under Income-tax Act to collect information related to full name, address and PAN of customer especially when, in preceding financial years, subsequent financial years and other periods of this same financial year, same practice was being followed by assessee- Held, yes - Whether therefore, sales could not be doubted on surmises and conjectures merely due to non-furnishing of address and PAN of customer - Held,yes - Whether therefore, addition made under section 68 in respect of unaccounted sale was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee engaged in jewellery business accumulated cash from sales, which was deposited in bank in demonetized currency, since assessee explained that said practice was in line with trend of cash deposits in past years which was accepted by department in assessments framed in past and future and no material was brought on record by revenue authorities to draw any adverse inference, addition made under section 68 in respect of unaccounted sale was to be deleted

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 65 of the VDIS, 1997 - Cash credit (Jewellery) - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee voluntarily disclosed gold and diamond jewellery under section 65(1) of VDIS, 1997 - Declaration as submitted by assessee came to be accepted by Commissioner and a certificate under section 68(2) of VDIS 1997 came to be issued - Subsequently, assessee filed return for relevant assessment year by declaring negative income from sale of above said VDIS declared gold and diamond jewellery items, which had been converted into bullion after smelting and separating diamonds through a goldsmith - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's claim and brought entire sale consideration of VDIS declared items to tax under section 68 - Tribunal upheld addition made by Assessing Officer - It was noted that Assessing Officer had not disputed weight or gold sold by assessee after smelting it from jeweller - Moreover, Tribunal in its various decisions in case of other assessee's who were similarly placed, had accepted capital gain declared on sale of VDIS declared items after smelting them through various jewellers - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, Tribunal committed an error in not accepting sale invoices submitted by assessee on ground that it was not same items which had been shown and declared by them in VDIS - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Where assessee having declared gold and diamond jewellery items under section 65(1) of VDIS, 1997, sold those items after smelting and separating diamonds through a goldsmith, in view of fact that there was no dispute about weight gold sold by assessee, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of aforesaid transaction was to be deleted

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Sale proceeds of jewellery) - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-HUF declared gold jewellery, silver and diamonds under VDIS, 1997 and paid taxes - Assessee converted jewellery into standard bullion and sold same - Invoices for jewellery conversion as well as sale bills of bullions were submitted - Whether mere change in nomenclature from jewellery in VDIS declaration to bullion in sale bills was not relevant and it was to be seen whether these were one and same - Held, yes - Whether since quantitative details also substantiate same, no addition as unexplained credit could be made - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11][In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Where assessee-HUF converted jewellery declared under VDIS into bullion and sold same, sale consideration received could not be considered as unexplained credit merely because nomenclature of items sold were different from that declared in VDIS

II. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained moneys (Purchase of Jewellery)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - In course of search and seizure operation, a pair of diamond bangles purchased from FI was found during search in case of assessee - Departmental valuer valued one bangle at Rs. 7.76 lakhs and left out other - Assessee in a statement under section 132(4) stated that pair of bangles was purchased for a consideration of Rs. 8.72 lakhs and also furnished supporting evidence by way of purchase bill - He further stated that other bangle left out by Departmental valuer was valued by another registered valuer at Rs. 4.39 lakhs and, hence, value of two bangles would work out to Rs. 8.78 lakhs, which was more or less equal to invoice value - However, Assessing Officer relying upon statement of an employee of FI added back an amount of Rs. 8.62 lakhs, being amount allegedly paid in cash over and above invoice value - Whether addition made to income of assessee under section 69A solely relying upon statement of a third party was not sustainable, more so, when assessee denied of having paid any cash - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition so made was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading of gold  diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. - Assessing Officer on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three parties were bogus - Accordingly, he made an addition - It was observed that assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers - Further, information gathered by Investigation Wing was based upon statements of persons who were managing affairs of assessee’s suppliers, however, these witnesses were not subject to cross examination - Whether, on facts, said purchases could not be treated as bogus and, therefore, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 26] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made an addition in hands of assessee on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three concerns were bogus purchases, since assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers etc., such purchases could not be treated as bogus

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]  Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer received information from investigation wing that assessee had debited expenses in form of commission from four different parties - Enquiries were conducted and found that all 4 companies had same address and they were not available on addresses mentioned in income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises - Based on said information, Assessing Officer disallowed commission expenses claimed by assessee - It was noted that all four entities were assessed by same Assessing Officer and commission income shown by them was accepted - It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where it was evident from certain seized papers that assessee purchased gold ornaments and jewellery and made investment in those items but no date or name was mentioned on said paper, in such a case, it could not be said that amount mentioned in seized papers was assessee’s unexplained investment
Devilal Gherilal Shah v. Dy. Commissioner [1995] 52 TTJ (Ahd.) 618
Where it was evident from certain seized papers that the assessee purchased gold ornaments and jewellery and made investment in those items but no date or name was mentioned on the said paper, in such a case it was very difficult to say that the assessee purchased gold ornaments and that, therefore, he should be assessed in respect of the amount mentioned therein as unexplained investment made by him.

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee in regard to purchase of jewellery during year stated that her relative purchased said jewellery for a function using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his agricultural income and savings - Whether since onus to prove genuineness of transaction, creditworthiness and identity lay with assessee and it was to be discharged with reasonable explanation which had not been put forward unequivocally by assessee and bill was also in name of assessee, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69 - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed that purchase of jewellery during year was made by her relative using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his savings, since onus to prove genuineness of transaction lay with assessee which had not been discharged, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69  INCOME TAX : Where assessee stated that during year she jointly purchased an immovable property along with a party and sale amount toward her share was paid by aforesaid party and it was given as interest free loan outstanding as loan as on date, since assessee had not furnished statement of affairs of aforesaid party to prove that she was a debtor in his books, Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly considered aforesaid amount as assessee's income from other sources

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits -  Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2001-02 - Assessee showed long-term losses on account of sale of jewellery in its original returns of income filed for assessment years under consideration - Jewellery was shown to be sold to 'S' and 'JJ' - Said jewellery was earlier declared by assessee under VDIS - Subsequently, Assessing Officer by relying upon findings of Commissioner of Customs and Central Excise, doubted genuineness and existence of those two parties as they were not found at their given addresses and, accordingly, made additions on account of bogus cash credits - On further appeal, Tribunal found that assessee had produced all necessary information about these transactions and abovenamed parties supported with documents like their permanent account numbers, bank accounts, their trade-tax assessment orders, sale vouchers issued by them against claimed sales as well as their full addresses - Assessee had also produced buyers income-tax returns for relevant years in which profits on sale of jewellery shown in respective returns were accepted by department - Sale considerations were also paid by them to assessee through account payee cheques - It, therefore, held that assessee had furnished all necessary information supported with documents about transactions and parties which could have been expected from a prudent seller to establish genuineness of claimed sales and, accordingly, deleted said additions - Whether Tribunal had given cogent reasons for arriving at its factual conclusion and same needed no interference - Held, yes

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 - Unexplained expenditure (Writ Jurisdiction) - Assessment year 2021-22 - Assessee had purchased huge quantum of bullion/jewellery from three sellers namely Shiv Sahai, Diamond and Surana for a sum of Rs. 234.15 crores - It had also paid commission to foreign and local agents for procuring buyers - Assessing Officer had disallowed aforesaid expenses and computed a sum of Rs. 240.18 crores as total income of petitioner for reason that petitioner could not produce any documentary proof to prove genuineness of said expenses - Assessee had filed a writ petition challenging order passed by Assessing Officer - It was observed that Surana was under liquidation and had sold jewellery to assessee pursuant to an auction conducted by Company Secretary appointed as Insolvency Resolution Professional - Assessee had attached sample invoice for a sum of Rs. 17.27 crores issued by Company Secretary, however, before Court it had filed copies of invoice for a sum of Rs. 127.35 crores - Further, although, during period dispute, movement of jewellery items including bullion were not required to accompany e-way bill in terms of rule 138(4)(a) of GST Rules, 2017, as amended by Notification No. 12/2018 - Central Tax with effect from 1-4-2018, assessee ought to have filed GST Returns of supplier and GST Returns in Form GST 2A - These documents were not furnished by assessee - And, issues regarding payment of commission to both Indian and foreign agents were not properly explained by assessee - Whether since there were several disputed question of facts which did not call for adjudication in a summary proceedings under article 226 of Constitution, writ was to be dismissed and assessee was to be given liberty to file a statutory appeals before Appellate Authority both against impugned assessment order - Held, yes [Paras 53 to 56] [In favour of revenue]   Circulars  Notifications : Notification No. 27/2017-Central Tax issued under respective GST Enactments for movement of Gold Bullion and Jewellery

Section 69A, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained Moneys (Demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery - During demonetization period, assessee deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers in its bank account - Assessing Officer observed that cash sales were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by assessee company merely to build an explanation for cash deposits in to bank account and made an addition of total cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE - Assessee furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for relevant period and cash sales made by assessee had been credited in books of account and, thus, assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences - Further, no defect had been pointed out in books of account of assessee - When sale had been offered to tax, adding same again would amount to double taxation - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving source of cash deposited in bank, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had paid commission to four entities on export of diamond and had furnished all relevant details in respect of said commission alongwith details of service tax collected thereon, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure as non-genuine and bogus

Section  69C,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing, buying and selling of jewellery - During relevant assessment year, assessee had entered into transactions with five parties - Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in books of assessee - Assessing Officer further presumed that assessee had earned additional gross profit by procuring diamonds from grey market and accordingly made addition being 8 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases -  Commissioner  (Appeals) restricted profit estimation to 3 per cent - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating detailed evidences filed by assessee including quantitative details, purchase and sales registers, bank statements, confirmations, sales-tax registration, and income-tax returns of supplier parties, came to conclusion that sales and closing stock figures were duly accepted by Assessing Officer - Commissioner (Appeals) further observed that without corresponding purchases, assessee could not have affected sales - Thus, only profit element embedded in such alleged purchases could be brought to tax, not entire purchase value - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly restricted addition to 3 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases was fair, reasonable and in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section  68,  read with section  206C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Illustrations)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee, engaged in retail jewellery trade, recorded a sale of 349.740 grams of gold jewellery valued at about Rs. 9.88 lakhs on 1-12-2016 to a customer - Against this sale, cash of about Rs. 6.92 lakhs was received on 31-3-2017 from jeweller and recorded in books; sales invoice and cash receipt were furnished - Assessing Officer never disbelieved documents submitted by assessee, however, made additions only on ground that assessee had not collected TCS under section 206C(1D) from the buyer of the gold jewellery - Whether since turnover of assessee from her business for preceding financial year 2015-16 relevant to assessment year 2016-17 was less than turnover limit fixed for getting accounts audited under section 44AB, provisions of Section 206C(1D) were not applicable for year under consideration and thus, addition made by Assessing Officer on wrong assumption of application of provisions of section 206C(1D), could not be upheld - Held, yes [Para 15] [In favour of assessee]

X. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Bullion)  - Assessment year  2023-24  - During search, a rough slip was found and confronted to assessee - In statement under section 132(4), assessee stated purchase of two gold coins of 100 grams each, admitted to have paid Rs.5 lakhs in cash to jewellers with balance of about Rs.11.50 lakhs pending - He explained source of Rs.5 lakhs as withdrawal from capital account in M/s Kalta Liquors and later furnished purchase bill and evidence that balance was paid through banking channels - Whether since assessee furnished ample evidences during course of assessment proceedings to substantiate its stand, this addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68,  read with sections  54  and  115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961/  Section  102 ,    read with  sections  86   and   195 , of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Cash Credit (Sale consideration)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee sold an immovable property and stated that cash deposits in her bank account during demonetisation were sourced from sale consideration comprising part by cheque and part in cash - Assessing Officer noted that notice issued under section 133(6) to purchaser was not complied with and assessee did not furnish complete sale deed - He further observed that agreement value of property was Rs.49 lakhs as against alleged receipt of Rs.74.50 lakhs, and that claim of receipt of additional cash was not reflected in the agreement - Accordingly, Assessing Officer treated cash portion as unexplained cash credit under section 68 - It was noted that assessee had claimed deduction under section 54 amounting to Rs.73.06 lakhs, which clearly established that transaction of sale of property was duly reported - It was also noted that assessee had furnished acknowledgements evidencing receipt of cash on different dates - It was further brought on record that part of payment was made directly by purchaser to developer on behalf of assessee, which had been acknowledged in writing - Further, assessee had placed on record notice issued under section 133(6) in case of purchaser along with reply wherein purchaser had categorically confirmed transaction and acknowledged payment of cash towards purchase of property - Whether since evidences furnished by assessee including third-party confirmation had remained uncontroverted, assessee had satisfactorily explained source of cash deposits and discharged onus cast upon her under provisions of Act - Held, yes - Whether, thus, addition made under section 68 was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 24 and 25] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69A of Income-tax Act, 1961
Others
Navinchandra M. Patel v. ITO [1992] 42 TTJ (Ahd.) 98 
In the course of raid conducted by custom authorities, the assessee was found in possession of certain diamonds to which the assessee explained that he took loans from two persons and out of the amount of loan he purchased those diamonds from several persons in the market whom he did not know and from whom he did not obtain any receipt. On enquiry by the custom officers those persons denied having lent any amount to the assessee. Then the assessee changed his version about the diamonds and stated that diamonds were received on approval basis under Jhangad receipts and he was not owner at the time of seizure. The ITO holding that there was no satisfactory explanation, assessed value of diamonds as income of the assessee.
Held that the source of the amount which was invested in acquiring diamonds was not proved by the assessee and as such addition was rightly made by the ITO.

Section 68 of the Income tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - During relevant assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer found that assessee had credited certain amount received on sale of diamonds, bullion and gold ornaments - Assessee was asked to furnish details like bills and details of jewellery - Assessee furnished valuation report of gold ornaments and diamonds and in respect of bullion he produced sold bill issued by 'M' and 'S' - Assessing Officer however, made addition under section 68 and, accordingly, levied penalty under section 274 read with 271(1)(c) and also levied interest under section 234B - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) allowed appeal of assessee - On second appeal, Tribunal held that transaction in respect of bullion sold to 'M' was not genuine as there was some irregularities in account of 'M' and accordingly, sustained addition in that respect - It was found from records that issue involved in instant case had already been considered by High Court in ITA No. 218/2004 by order dated 23-9-2008 whereby matter had been remitted to Assessing Officer to pass fresh orders insofar as it related to sale of jewellery to 'M' - Whether therefore, issue involved in instant case was to be decided by following abovesaid order of High Court - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Sales during demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee was engaged in business of ornaments and jewellery (of gold, silver & diamond) - During demonetisation, assessee made cash sales of Rs. 10.28 crores on 08-11-2016 - Assessing Officer accepted cash sale of Rs. 76 lakhs as genuine but disbelieved remaining amount of Rs. 9.24 crores and added same to income of assessee under section 68 - It was noted that no specific transaction of sale, not even one, had been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue - Allegation of Revenue holding that cash sales of aforesaid amount claimed by assessee to be untrue, was without convincing materials - Aforesaid addition had been made by Revenue based merely on suspicion, doubt, conjecture and guess work - Assessee had provided convincing material to show that it had sufficient stock, sufficient man power and sufficient time to make aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.24 crores even after announcement of demonetisation - Moreover, assessee had shown sales in VAT returns, which had been accepted by VAT authorities - Whether, on facts, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Para E.2.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

Section  68  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  102  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Cash Credit (Cash deposits) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee, engaged in jewellery business, deposited cash of Rs. 35 lakh during demonetisation period - Assessing Officer treated Rs. 19.50 lakh as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that there was abnormal increase in cash sales during October 2016 and some cash sales were made to unidentified persons - It was noted that no discrepancy was found in assessee's audited books of account, VAT returns, cash book, stock register, purchase register or sales register - It was further noted that assessee had established a direct nexus between cash sales, stock movement and cash deposits, and Assessing Officer had neither disturbed stock records nor rejected sales - Whether once AO had accepted sales and assessee had substantially established on basis of financials that there was a direct nexus of cash sales with closing stock, then addition under section 68 was not justified - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Demonetization) - Assessment year  2017-18 - During demonetization period, assessee-jeweller deposited huge amount in three bank accounts - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had suddenly made cash sales to unidentifiable small customers during period from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - He, therefore, made addition under section 68 on account of such unexplained cash credit (sales) - It was noted that business of assessee was an expanding business and sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over years - Assessee had furnished before Assessing Officer month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and movement in stock position - Details of stock, purchases and sales that had been submitted by assessee before Assessing Officer had not been questioned or doubted in any manner by Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee had presented evidence of available stock and depletion of said stock on account of sales and Assessing Officer had not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of receipts on account of sale of that stock were unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 was made out - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C, read with sections 40A(3) and 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading and manufacturing of diamonds - Assessee made purchases from certain tainted dealers - Assessing Officer concluded that assessee made purchases from grey market to save indirect taxes and, thus, incidental profit element which was embedded in value of said purchases was to be brought to tax - He, thus, estimated profit element embedded in value of disputed purchases at 5 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced same to 3 per cent - It was noted that report of Task Force for Diamond Sector constituted by Ministry of Commerce and Industry recommended that net profit prevailing in diamond industry engaged in business of trading would be in range of 1 per cent to 3 per cent and those engaged in business of manufacturing would be in range of 1.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent - Whether since Tribunal had consistently taken stand by estimating profit element on basis of reliance placed on report of Task Force, Commissioner (Appeals) was duly justified in estimating profit percentage of 3 per cent - Held, yes [Para 4.2] [In favour of revenue]

Section 69C, read with sections 40A(3) and 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading and manufacturing of diamonds - Assessee made purchases from certain tainted dealers - Assessing Officer concluded that assessee made purchases from grey market to save indirect taxes and, thus, incidental profit element which was embedded in value of said purchases was to be brought to tax - He, thus, estimated profit element embedded in value of disputed purchases at 5 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced same to 3 per cent - It was noted that report of Task Force for Diamond Sector constituted by Ministry of Commerce and Industry recommended that net profit prevailing in diamond industry engaged in business of trading would be in range of 1 per cent to 3 per cent and those engaged in business of manufacturing would be in range of 1.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent - Whether since Tribunal had consistently taken stand by estimating profit element on basis of reliance placed on report of Task Force, Commissioner (Appeals) was duly justified in estimating profit percentage of 3 per cent - Held, yes [Para 4.2] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of trading and manufacturing of diamonds, made purchases from certain tainted dealers, in view of report of Task Force for Diamond Sector constituted by Ministry of Commerce and Industry, profit element embedded in value of disputed purchases for diamond manufacturers was to be estimated in range of 1.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent
Section 6(2), read with section 27 of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 - Pledging of gold ornaments must be proved before action. So also the SALE has to be proved-else Benefit of Doubt must be given

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - On basis of statement of one ‘V’ recorded during survey conducted in his proprietary concern ‘D’, Assessing Officer treated sale of diamonds by 
 assessee to ‘D’ as fictitious and made addition under section 68 in hands of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld addition - Whether no opportunity of cross-examining ‘V’ having been allowed to assessee, statement of ‘V’ could be relied upon and could be made basis of addition - Held, no - Whether no doubt onus of proving sale of diamonds lay on assessee, but assessee having depended upon Assessing Officer for effecting presence of ‘V’ for cross-examination and Assessing Officer having not taken appropriate steps for enforcing attendance of ‘V’, Assessing Officer could not make addition in hands of assessee on ground that assessee had failed to produce ‘V’ - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition was to be deleted - Held, yes

II. Section 69C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2011-12, 2012-13 and 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged in trading and manufacture of silver, gold, diamonds, stones and its jewellery - During assessment, Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases - Commissioner (Appeals) observed that though two entities were found to be bogus, assessee had, in fact, purchased diamonds which were used for purpose of making diamond jewellery and, therefore, sale of such diamond jewellery had been accepted by Assessing Officer - He further observed that assessee had shown from its audited books of account, stock statement as well as material receipt register that it could not have sold equivalent quantum of diamond jewellery without these two purchases - He, therefore, found it reasonable to disallow 3 per cent of total purchases from bogus Hawala concerns and reduced addition - Tribunal confirmed view of Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether once purchases are accepted, difference between inflated and actual price of purchases would be required to be disallowed and as to what would be extent of difference would be a matter of estimate - Held, yes - Whether estimate made by two appellate authorities did not warrant interference as, even otherwise, whether estimate should be at a particular sum or at a different sum, can never be an issue of law - Held, yes [Para 4.8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was a legal heir of 'W' - During relevant assessment year, assessee filed his return showing loss arising from sale of diamond jewellery belonging to 'W' - In order to prove genuineness of sales transactions, assessee produced sale invoices and submitted that sale consideration had been received through account payee cheques - Assessing Officer rejected documentary evidence furnished by assessee and concluded that no such sale of jewellery took place - He thus treated amount of sales deposited in bank as income from unexplained sources - Tribunal confirmed order of Assessing Officer - It was apparent from records that nothing had been disclosed in respect of jewellery in assessee's wealth tax returns - Moreover, evidence which had been produced was of recent origin in form of sale invoice or report of valuer but initial onus placed upon assessee was not discharged by providing unimpeachable evidence - Whether on facts, assessee failed to prove that sales transactions in question were genuine and, therefore, impugned addition made by Tribunal was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee, a legal heir of 'W', declared certain loss arising from sale of jewellery belonging to 'W', in view of fact that nothing had been disclosed in respect of said jewellery in Wealth tax return, sale in question being bogus, sale amount deposited in bank was to be treated as assessee's income from unexplained sources
Section 34 of the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 - Dealing with a person believing him to be an agent of a dealer is no offence

Section 69A of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee had returned capital gains arising from sale of gold jewellery allegedly made out of gold received as gift from his wife, merely because there was a difference of one carat between gold received as gift and jewellery sold, entire sale proceeds could not be treated as undisclosed investment of assessee
Hari Chand v. ITO [1983] 17 TTJ (Asr.) 141
Where the assessee had returned capital gains arising from the sale of gold jewellery allegedly made out of gold received as gift from his wife, merely because there was a difference of one carat between gold received as gift and jewellery sold, entire sale proceeds could not be treated as undisclosed investment of the  assessee.

Section 69 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee claimed that gold jewellery seized from her locker was received as gift during her marriage long back, in absence of proof by department that jewellery was purchased in year in question, addition on basis of price of gold in year in question as undisclosed investment was not justified
Shakuntala Devi Saraf v. ITO [1988] 31 TTJ (Jp.) 9
During the assessment year 1982-83 old jewellery were seized from the locker of the assessee and an addition on account of income from undisclosed sources representing investment in jewellery was made. The assessee’s case was that the jewellery were given to her by her father and in-laws at the time of marriage in 1963. She requested the department to inspect the jewellery to satisfy as to whether they were purchased in the year in question or were old so as to clear the doubt of the department regarding investment in year in question. The revenue, however, merely on the basis that the financial position of the assessee's father after two years of the assessee’s marriage was not sound, rejected the explanation of the assessee.
Held, that the authorities rejected the plea of the assessee regarding inspecting of the ornaments for determining whether they were old or new which could have helped in removing any possible doubts in the minds of the department. There was no evidence available on the file of the revenue to indicate that there had been any purchases by the assessee of jewellery in the relevant previous year. Merely for the reason that the price of gold had increased at the time of making of the assessment or at the time of hearing of the appeal should not be kept as a base for deciding any such investment as it would only result in a distorted picture, especially when there was no evidence available to indicate that the acquisition was in the relevant previous year of appeal. Addition was made without any basis and was, therefore, deleted.

IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 - Unexplained expenditure (Writ Jurisdiction) - Assessment year 2021-22 - Assessee had purchased huge quantum of bullion/jewellery from three sellers namely Shiv Sahai, Diamond and Surana for a sum of Rs. 234.15 crores - It had also paid commission to foreign and local agents for procuring buyers - Assessing Officer had disallowed aforesaid expenses and computed a sum of Rs. 240.18 crores as total income of petitioner for reason that petitioner could not produce any documentary proof to prove genuineness of said expenses - Assessee had filed a writ petition challenging order passed by Assessing Officer - It was observed that Surana was under liquidation and had sold jewellery to assessee pursuant to an auction conducted by Company Secretary appointed as Insolvency Resolution Professional - Assessee had attached sample invoice for a sum of Rs. 17.27 crores issued by Company Secretary, however, before Court it had filed copies of invoice for a sum of Rs. 127.35 crores - Further, although, during period dispute, movement of jewellery items including bullion were not required to accompany e-way bill in terms of rule 138(4)(a) of GST Rules, 2017, as amended by Notification No. 12/2018 - Central Tax with effect from 1-4-2018, assessee ought to have filed GST Returns of supplier and GST Returns in Form GST 2A - These documents were not furnished by assessee - And, issues regarding payment of commission to both Indian and foreign agents were not properly explained by assessee - Whether since there were several disputed question of facts which did not call for adjudication in a summary proceedings under article 226 of Constitution, writ was to be dismissed and assessee was to be given liberty to file a statutory appeals before Appellate Authority both against impugned assessment order - Held, yes [Paras 53 to 56] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where there were several disputed question of facts as regards commission paid by assessee to foreign and local agents for procuring buyers and expenditure incurred for purchase of bullion/jewellery which did not call for adjudication in a summary proceedings under article 226 of Constitution, writ petition filed by assessee was to be dismissed

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Cash deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee had made cash deposit during demonetization period in her bank account - Assessing Officer held that cash sales shown by assessee during period of 10 days just before demonetization was not genuine but fabricated and after thought being colourable device used to show unaccounted cash as accounted one - Thus, Assessing Officer made addition of said amount under section 68 - It was noted that Assessing Officer had accepted transactions about purchase and sale of jewellery in gold and silver without raising any doubt regarding books of account, purchase and sale stock registers and bills produced by assessee - Further, cash transaction before demonetization period was also revealed by assessee as period before demonetization was also period of Diwali and that itself showed that why cash transaction took place in that particular period - Whether since stock register as well as family evidences produced by assessee were found to be genuine and cash transaction had also been proved by assessee being genuine transaction, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 269A-269S of Income-tax Act, 1961
Gurbux Kaur Sandhu v. IAC [1983] 15 TTJ (Chd.) 128
It is not open to competent authority to draw any presumption under section 269C(1) prior to initiation of acquisition proceedings.

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified

facts.text:
■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee filed her return under VDIS, 1997, in which she declared sale proceeds of jewellery and diamonds received from two purchasers ‘G’ and ‘T’. The Commissioner accepted the return filed by the assessee and issued the certificate as envisaged under the VDIS. At a later stage, searches were conducted on those purchasers in which they conceded before the search party that no purchases were made by them and cheques had been issued after taking cash through the middlemen. Later on ‘T’ retracted from his statement and confirmed that he had purchased jewellery from the assessee. On the basis of statements of both the purchasers, the Assessing Officer reopened the assessment and added the sale proceeds of jewelleries to the income of the assessee under section 68, and he made further addition at the rate of 3 per cent of both those amounts towards commission payments under section 69C. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted both the additions made by the Assessing Officer under sections 68 and 69C.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee submitted his return of income which, inter alia, included capital gains on sale of gold and jewellery. He availed the benefit of Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 and declared gold and diamond and necessary certificate under the said Scheme was issued by the Commissioner. Later, the assessee sold the gold and diamonds separately to ‘A’ and ‘S’, respectively. The sale of gold was accepted as genuine by the Assessing Officer, while the sale of diamonds to ‘S’ was not accepted as genuine and entire sale value thereof was added under section 68 by the Assessing Officer treating the same as unexplained credit. Accordingly, assessment was completed. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. A search was conducted on the KP group on 15-1-2020, the assessee’s case was centralized, and assessment for the year of search was framed under section 143(3).

■

In the assessment, the Assessing Officer derecognized the declared long-term capital gains and treated the sale consideration of diamonds of about Rs. 82.67 crores as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The Assessing Officer also made a consequential addition for alleged commission expenditure under section 69C at 0.18 per cent of the sale consideration, amounting to about Rs. 14.88 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowed the appeal by confirming the addition under section 68 of about Rs. 82.67 crores on account of sale of diamonds and the addition under section 69C of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs on account of alleged commission expenditure.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

The Assessing Officer made an addition under section 68 in hands of the assessee on account of unexplained cash credit on the basis of survey in the case of one ‘V’ and his statement recorded then. The Assessing Officer had treated the sale of diamonds by assessee to ‘D’ as fictitious merely on the statement of ‘V’, the proprietor of ‘D’. According to the assessee, no opportunity of cross-examining ‘V’ was allowed, and also ‘V’ through his affidavit, had since retracted from his statement recorded during survey. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-firm was engaged in business of trading in bullion, jewellery, etc.

■

Based on information/material found during the search and seizure/ survey operations in case of partners of assessee-firm the departmental authorities observed that large amount of cash was deposited in various bank accounts of different entities, which, after layering were transferred to the assessee. The Assessing Officer found that as per the investigation carried out by the Investigation Wing, the assessee had purportedly sold gold and bullions to 44 entities controlled and managed by an entry operator, namely, Sonu Punjabi, which were sham transactions carried out during the demonetization period. It was alleged by the Assessing Officer that though notices under section 133(6) as well as summons under section 131 were issued, no information came from such entities as most of the summons returned back unserved. The Assessing Officer finally concluded that sales of gold/bullion to 44 entities allegedly controlled by Sonu Punjabi, were bogus sales and made for the purpose of introducing own money routed through bogus firms to its accounts. Thus, he treated the amount credited to the books of account as receipts from sale of gold/bullion, as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

The Assessing Officer further observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of gold/bullion worth Rs. 20.87 crore to RBPL and that in course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of M of RBPL statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he allegedly stated that cash amounting to Rs. 32.81 crore given to him by a firm, namely, DL Jewellers was deposited in the bank account of RBPL, for the purpose of transferring the fund to specific accounts on commission basis. The Assessing Officer ultimately concluded that the purported sales of gold/bullion to RBPL was bogus. Accordingly, he treated the receipt from sale of gold/bullion to RBPL as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee.

■

Further, the Assessing Officer observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of Rs. 19.30 lakhs to Olivia, towards sale of gold/ bullion. He observed that in course of survey conducted in the case of Olivia, it was found that the said company was incorporated in January 2015 and in assessment year 2015-16 it had filed the return of income offering NIL income without any turnover whereas, huge amount of cash was found to have been deposited in the bank account of Olivia, which suggested that the entity was an entry provider. Accordingly, he treated the amount in dispute as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee. Similarly, he treated receipts from S.S Overseas as bogus sales and held it as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member, having found that the assessee was able to establish the identity and creditworthiness of the entities purchasing gold/bullion from the assessee as well as the genuineness of the transactions, held that not only the sales were genuine but none of the conditions of section 68 were applicable to the subject transactions. Accordingly, he deleted the entire addition. Whereas, the Judicial Member did not agree with the view expressed by the Accountant Member. He was of the view that not only the sales were bogus but the amount representing bogus sales was required to be added to the business income by treating them as unexplained investment under section 69. Thus, the Judicial Member directed the Assessing Officer to convert the disputed addition from section 68 to section 69.

■

On reference to Third Member :

The assessees were dealers in diamonds. Each of the assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997. The said declarations were accepted by the Department and a certificate was issued to the respective assessees under the VDIS, 1997. The assessees claimed to have sold the jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 in the year relevant to the assessment year 1998-99 and offered to tax the capital gains arising from the respective sales. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque.
