While reading penal provisions for the purpose of understanding them, one should pay attention to what is "said" in the section(s) as also what is "not said" in the section(s), what is "intended" to be said in the section(s) and so also what is "not intended" to be said in the section(s). One should basically refer to the provisions of the relevant sections and then refer to the relevant Finance Bill, the Memorandum explaining the reasons for such amendment, the speech of the Finance Minister while moving the Finance Bill where there has been an explanation with regard to amendment to a particular Section including substitution of a particular Section and then to Board Circular, if any expressing the intention of the Legislature. After referring to these aspects then reference should be made to judicial decisions to find out or ensure whether a particular issue obtaining/arising in the given case has arisen earlier and decided by the judicial authorities.

At any cost, thorough preparation is required while handling the cases of assessees (clients). One has to update himself on a daily basis and especially with so many ITAT Benches, number of judgments (orders) coming out of these Benches is so large that one should ensure that important judicial pronouncements do not escape his attention.

Taking a cue from the examples, is it not interesting that, as per the Prevention of Money Laundering Act of 2002, dealers who deal in gold and precious metals are considered reporting entities?

Applicability of Reporting Requirements.

The government of any country is required to monitor all points of entry, or legal or white channels of transaction, via which black money might be transformed into white money. Jewellery shops are the most common access points for laundering money due to its ease of accessibility and lesser compliance frameworks. To curb these risk factors and to check mate the flow of black money, necessary steps were taken by the government to include the dealers in precious metals to the ambit of the reporting entity.

Background

Notification no G.S.R 799(E) [F NO P-12011/14/2020-ES CELL DOR ] DATED 28.12.2020 says that 2020 In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-clause (iv) of clause (sa) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 (15 of 2003), the Central Government hereby notifies the dealers in precious metals, precious stones as persons carrying on designated businesses or professions - if they engage in any cash transactions with a customer equal to or above Rupees ten lakhs, carried out in a single operation or in several operations that appear to be linked.

Relevance

This means that where a dealer engages in any cash transaction with a customer equal to or above rupees ten lakhs, carried out in a single operation or in several operations that appear to be linked, then the dealer comes under the purview of reporting entity under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act ,2002.

Definitions

Reporting Entity

As per Sec 2 (1) (wa) of Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 "reporting entity" means a banking company, financial institution, intermediary or a person carrying on a designated business or profession;

Designated Business or Profession is defined under Sec 2 (1)(sa) of Prevention of Money Laundering Act of 2002 which says that

"person carrying on designated business or profession" means,—

a person carrying on activities for playing games of chance for cash or kind, and includes such activities associated with casino;

real estate agent, as may be notified by the Central Government;

person carrying on such other activities as the Central Government may, by notification, so designate, from time to time;

CAPITAL GAINS*

5.1 Amendment to the definition of capital asset [Section 2(14)]

Capital gains under section 45 are chargeable on profits and gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset. The definition of capital asset in section 2(14) has been amended with effect from assessment year 2016-17 so as to exclude Deposit Certificates issued under Gold Monetisation Scheme, 2015 notified by the Central Government [section 2(14)(vi)].

Thus, the term 'capital asset' does not include such deposit certificates and any gains arising upon transfer of the certificate is exempt from capital gains tax.

The loss, if any, upon transfer of certificates will also not be taken into consideration. To illustrate, suppose the cost of acquisition of a deposit certificate is Rs. 3.3 lakh and the realization after 3 years is Rs. 3 lakh (owing to reduction in market value of gold). In such a case, the loss of Rs. 30,000 cannot be claimed as set off against other gains/income.

The exemption would be available to both, the initial subscriber of the deposit certificate as well as subsequent buyer of the certificate.

5.1-1 No immunity from taxation under section 69, etc.

There is no immunity from taxation under section 69, etc. under Chapter VI. To illustrate, if the assessee has converted bullion into deposit certificate and it is found that the bullion is not recorded in the books of account and the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source of acquisition of the bullion, then the value of the bullion may be deemed to be the income of the assessee under section 69A. This is also supported by the clarification in Office Memorandum [F. No.20/6/2015-FT], dated 15-9-2015 issued by the Government of India which states that 'further, the depositors may be informed by the banks that as per CBDT Instruction No. 1916 dated 11th May, 1994 in course of IT Search u/s 132, gold jewellery to the extent of 500 gms per married lady, 250 gms per unmarried lady and 100 gms per male member of the family, need not be seized by tax authorities, but the tax penalties, as applicable will be levied.'

Thus, tax penalties as applicable may be levied, if the assessee is not able to satisfactorily explain the source of acquisition of bullion.

5.1-2 Cost of acquisition of gold received on exchange of Gold Bonds at the time of the redemption.

There are two types of gold deposit schemes:

(a)

Short Term Bank Deposit (STBD)

(b)

Medium and Long Term Government Deposit (MLTGD)

The redemption of MLTGD will be only in Indian Rupee equivalent to the value of the gold.

In respect of STBD, redemption of principal and interest at maturity will, at the option of the depositor, be either in Indian Rupee equivalent of the deposited gold and accrued interest based on the price of gold prevailing at the time of redemption, or in gold.

The questions that arise are —

(a)

What is the cost of the gold for the purpose of determining capital gains upon its eventual transfer?

(b)

What is the date of acquisitions of the gold for the purposes of its treatment as short term capital asset or otherwise?

In 1965, the Government of India had issued National Defence Gold Bonds, 1980. These Bonds were redeemable after 15 years, that is, on or after 2-10-1980. In this connection, the CBDT had clarified as follows videCircular No. 415, dated 14-3-1985. 'A question has arisen as to whether such capital gains should be treated as long-term or short-term capital gains. The question has been examined by the Board. The exchange of gold bonds at the time of redemption is an altogether fresh transaction when an assessee acquires a different asset. It has also been decided above that for the purposes of the computation of capital gains, cost of acquisition of gold would be the market value of the bonds on the date of redemption. The material date in this case would, therefore, be the date of redemption of gold bonds which would be treated as the date of acquisition of the gold. As per section 2(42A) 'short-term capital asset' means a capital asset held by an assessee for not more than 36 months immediately preceding the date of transfer. The question as to whether the gains arising in such cases would be short or long-term would, therefore, depend upon the time that has passed between the date of redemption of gold bonds and the subsequent sale of gold.'

The income based on the books of account of ‘V’ was accepted in his case under the Act which included the said transaction. [Para 25]

Similarly, ‘V’ being the registered dealer under the BST and CST Act had filed the returns under those Acts, duly disclosing the said transaction with the assessee much before the date of survey. [Para 26] The observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that since ‘V’ was denying the explanation given at the time of survey, it was upon him to explain the cash deposits in his bank accounts and the lack of closing stock was not convincing. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The two statements were conflicting and as to for which statement he said ‘remained’, was not known. It would be more logical, if it was so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000, which was confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. [Para 27]

The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. [Para 28]

The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath, recorded by the Assessing Officer, ‘V’ claiming that while he knew ‘S’, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, could not raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs.10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as ‘hawala’ transaction in the statement given to the department. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. [Para 30]

It was true that at the time of survey, it was not the case of ‘V’ that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants, but the fact remained that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee was concerned throughout. [Para 31]

Large amounts of cash were deposited in various bank accounts of ‘D’ on various dates by ‘R’, but there was no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there was no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32]

The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

11.11.4 Bullion or Jewellery:

With effect from 1-7-2012 under new sub-section (1D), sale of bullion/jewellery will be subject to TCS provisions, if the following conditions are satisfied —

♦ Sale consideration of bullion (excluding any coin/article weighing 10 grams or less) exceeds Rs. 2,00,000 or sale consideration of jewellery exceeds Rs. 5,00,000.

♦ Out of sale consideration any amount is received in cash.

If the above conditions are satisfied, the seller will collect tax at the rate of 1 per cent of sale consideration. Tax will be collected at the time of receipt of any amount in cash. This rule will be applicable irrespective of the fact whether the buyer is a manufacturer, trader or the purchase is for personal use. It covers any person implying a manufacturer or a dealer or an ultimate consumer. The person must obtain by way of sale, bullion or jewellery. In other words, to a transaction other than sale, the provisions of the sub-section (1D) would not apply.

11.11.5 Interest under section 206C(7)

Section 206C(7) provides for payment of simple interest in case of failure to collect whole or any part of tax, or after collecting payment thereof, by a person responsible for collecting tax.

Finance Act, 2012 inserts first proviso in section 206C(6A) (see para 11.8.4) to provide that in the circumstances specified therein the person shall not be deemed to be Assessee in default.

To charge the interest under sub-section (7) even in case of Assessee not deemed to be default, Finance Act, 2012 inserts a proviso in sub-section (7), effective 1-7-2012.

It provides that a person not deemed to be an assessee in default under the first proviso to sub-section (6A), who has failed to collect whole or any part of tax on any amount collected, would be liable to pay interest from the date on which the tax was collectible to the date of furnishing of return of income by a buyer etc.

To illustrate, the person was obliged to collect tax, say, on January 1. The buyer, etc., furnishes the return of income on July 31. The amount not collected by way of tax, say, is, say, Rs. 10,000. The person would be liable to pay interest on Rs. 10,000 for the period January 1 to July 31.

11.12 Fees for default in furnishing statements in respect of tax deductible or collectible:

Presently, section 272A(2)(k) provides for penalty for late filing of TDS and TCS statements, respectively, under section 200(3) and proviso to section 206C(3) ('TDS/TCS statements').

11.12.1 Amendment

Finance Act, 2012 has made the said provision inoperative and substituted the same by two new provisions:

(a) Section 234E providing for payment of fees for late filing of TDS/TCS statements; and

(b) Section 271H of the Act providing for larger penalty for the said default. (see para 13.5)

The old provision is made inoperative from 1-7-2012 and hence would apply in respect of defaults committed prior thereto. The new provisions apply in respect of obligations arising from and after 1-7-2012.

11.12.1a Salient provisions for the fees:

(a) A person is obliged to deliver or caused to be delivered TDS/TCS statements within specified time (see paras 13.5.1 and 13.5.2).

(b) He fails to deliver TDS/TCS statements.

(c) If so, he is liable to pay by way of fee Rs. 200 for every day of the default and till it continues.

(d) The amount of fees shall not exceed the amount of tax deductible or collectible.

(e) The fees shall be paid before delivering TDS/TCS statements.

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. [Para 13]

Thus, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit in the bank account and consequently sources of incurring expenditure by way of purchases claimed by the assessee in its profit and loss account of Rs. 48.78 crores could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee and onus cast under section 69C was not satisfied which would make amount covered by such expenditure represented by purchases of gold bars to be deemed income of the assessee under the deeming fiction of section 69C. The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. Thus, revenue succeeds on this ground while the assessee fails on this issue in their respective appeals. [Para 10]

Section 54 does not mandate that for claiming deduction filing of the claim in the return is a mandatory condition. Further, without going into the controversy as to whether the above transaction regarding long-term capital gain in respect of Lucknow property and the investment in Delhi property for claiming deduction under section 54 was intentional or unintentional, the fact remains that as per the provisions of section 45, the capital gains arising on the sale of Lucknow property shall inter alia be effected in the previous year save as otherwise provided in section 54. [Para 9.1]

■

The computation of capital gains as filed by the assessee regarding sale consideration of Rs. 45.95 lakhs of the Lucknow property and the indexation cost of Rs. 28.82 lakhs claimed by the assessee resulting in capital gain of Rs. 17.13 lakhs has not been disputed by the Assessing Officer. Regarding the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the property at Lucknow was sold in financial year 2013-14 and it could not be adjusted against the execution of the property at New Delhi, which was purchased on 21-2-2005, it is not acceptable in view of the fact that the receipt dated 21-2-2005 was only an ‘Agreement to Sell’, which went into the litigation as discussed above and the property was finally purchased by the assessee vide sale deed dated 23-12-2013. As per the submissions of the assessee, the assessee states that in year 2005, the possession of property at New Delhi was neither allowed to be retained by the assessee and rather the possession was taken on the date of registration of the sale deed, i.e., 23-12-2013. [Para 9.2]

■

In view of the above facts, it is held that the denial of deduction under section 54 by the Assessing Officer for the reasons as stated above and the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Delhi property was acquired as purchased on 21-2-2005 is not correct. As noted above that in the respect of the long-term capital gains of Rs. 17.13 lakhs in respect of sale of property at Lucknow, a sum of Rs. 22.30 lakhs was paid by the assessee for the purchase of the new property at Delhi as per the requirement under section 54. Therefore, as per the provision of section 45(1) and section 54(1)(ii), the assessee will be entitled for deduction under section 54 as claimed by him since the amount of long-term capital gain of Rs. 17.13 lakhs is less than the purchase cost of Rs. 22.30 lakhs paid by the assessee for the new property being Delhi, which was paid one year prior to the purchase of the property Lucknow, as required under the said provisions. Accordingly, it is held that the assessee is entitled for deduction for long-term capital gain of Rs. 17.13 lakhs under section 54 and therefore the addition of Rs. 17.13 lakhs made by the Assessing Officer and confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) is deleted. [Para 9.3]

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ In any given case, whether the sales claimed by the assessee are genuine or not, is a question of fact and the answer will depend on specific facts and circumstances of the case. In the present case, the addition has been made, disbelieving the assessee's claim that cash sales in SBNs were made, amounting to Rs. 9.25 crores on 8-11-2016. The case of revenue rests essentially on hypothesis that it was unlikely, based on materials available on record, surrounding circumstances, human conduct, preponderance of probabilities and nature of incriminating information/evidence available on record, that cash sales amounting to aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores were made in SBNs on 8-11-2016. No specific transaction of sale, not even one, has been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue. In fact the Assessing Officer himself has treated sale amounting to Rs. 75.99 lakhs (made in SBNs) to be genuine but has disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.25 crores. In the absence of any direct evidence to show that any specific sale transaction was not genuine or untrue, the question of fact before us is whether in the given facts and circumstances it is possible that the assessee might have made sale of aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores in cash on 8-11-2016. It is quite understandable, that after announcement of demonetization, the people in possession of SBNs were desperate to use it for purchase of gold, diamond and silver jewellery and other items before the deadline after which SBNs could not have been used. In such a desperate situation, it is quite understandable that customers would not exercise choice in selection as they might have done in normal course. Therefore, the submissions made from assessee's side that the customers instantly purchased whatever they saw on the counter, using SBNs, is acceptable. Further it is quite understandable that the assessee brought additional manpower to deal with and to attend to the extraordinary rush of customers. Therefore, the submission made from the assessee's side that family members, relatives, friends and staff of other business entities were utilized to attend the extraordinary rush of customers is also acceptable. It is not in dispute that the aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.25 crores included sale amounting to Rs. 1.67 crores which attracted penalty under section 271DA for contravention of section 269ST. Further it is not in dispute that the aforesaid total sales of Rs. 1.67 crores (consisting of each transaction exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs in cash) were not made through serially numbered sales vouchers. Instead, these transactions were interspersed with other sale transactions in cash, below Rs. 2 lakhs. These facts clearly establish that the sales claimed by the assessee to have been made in cash were genuine. Moreover, the contention that if the assessee had any intention to book bogus sales, then the assessee would not have booked sales inviting penalty under section 271BA is a reasonable one. It is further seen that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the assessee's books of account. Moreover, the assessee has shown the sales in VAT returns, which have been accepted by VAT authorities. It is not in dispute that the assessee had sufficient stock in trade to make sale as claimed, on 8-11-2016. Revenue has not doubted the purchases made by the assessee. Further not even a single specific sale transaction has been proved to be fake, bogus or untrue.

The assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during the demonetization and claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration.

The Assessing Officer issued show cause notice to assessee with respect to cash deposited in bank during demonetization. The Assessing Officer after verifying the details opined that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format. He thus, held that claim made by assessee remained unexplained and accordingly, made addition treating same as undisclosed income under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition made by Assessing Officer on ground that the assessee failed to discharge its onus of providing item-wise sale for each invoice especially for the month of November, 2016 and the fact that average per day sale in 39 days from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 was Rs. 20.87 lakhs as compared to Rs. 53,514/- only in financial year 2017-18 points to the fact that claim of cash sales was an afterthought to justify huge cash deposits in bank account during the demonetization period.

On appeal to the Tribunal.

■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, filed its return of income.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that during the demonetization period, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 3.80 crores in three bank accounts. He further noted that the assessee had made total sales of Rs. 49.99 crores during the financial year 2016-17 and the total cash sales during the year amounted to Rs. 4.94 crores. However, of the total cash sales, the assessee had made cash sales of Rs. 3.68 crores in October, 2016 and of Rs. 37.25 lakhs uptil 8.11.2016 i.e. in the period between 1.10.2016 to 8.11.2016, the assessee had suddenly made cash sales to the tune of Rs. 4.05 crores to unidentifiable small customers.He held that the assessee had not satisfactorily explained the credit of Rs. 3.68 crores recorded as cash sales in his books during the period 1.10.2016 to 30.10.2016, he held the same to be unexplained under section 68

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had not established that the assessee had accumulated cash in its books which was deposited on 10-11-2016. The assumptions made on the basis of comparison of sales figures of earlier years were not foolproof, as similar or higher sales had been made by the assessee in following financial year and the refusal to accept the sales shown by the assessee was not on account of any independent enquiry but only on the basis of assumptions/interpretations made by the Assessing Officer while comparing results of earlier years.

■

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition of Rs. 2.98 crores on account of unexplained cash deposit.

Section 69A of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee had returned capital gains arising from sale of gold jewellery allegedly made out of gold received as gift from his wife, merely because there was a difference of one carat between gold received as gift and jewellery sold, entire sale proceeds could not be treated as undisclosed investment of assessee
Hari Chand v. ITO [1983] 17 TTJ (Asr.) 141
Where the assessee had returned capital gains arising from the sale of gold jewellery allegedly made out of gold received as gift from his wife, merely because there was a difference of one carat between gold received as gift and jewellery sold, entire sale proceeds could not be treated as undisclosed investment of the  assessee.

The certificate issued by the revenue under the VDIS, 1997 to the effect that the assessee had diamond jewellery weighing 65.75 carats continued to be valid and subsisting and no proceedings had been initiated by the revenue till relevant time to cancel the certificate. [Para 12]

When the assessee claimed that the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 had been sold to T for Rs. 10,35,562, the same was accepted in the original assessment. However, in the reassessment order, the claim was disbelieved mainly by relying on the statement of 'T' recorded on 31-3-2000, wherein he had stated that the transactions recorded in his books were hawala transactions. It was further held that the above statement was corroborated by the non-availability of the diamond jewellery allegedly sold by the assessee to T and the bank accounts of T showed that he had received cash before issuing cheques to various parties including the assessee. [Para 13]

T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

Section 69 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee claimed that gold jewellery seized from her locker was received as gift during her marriage long back, in absence of proof by department that jewellery was purchased in year in question, addition on basis of price of gold in year in question as undisclosed investment was not justified
Shakuntala Devi Saraf v. ITO [1988] 31 TTJ (Jp.) 9
During the assessment year 1982-83 old jewellery were seized from the locker of the assessee and an addition on account of income from undisclosed sources representing investment in jewellery was made. The assessee’s case was that the jewellery were given to her by her father and in-laws at the time of marriage in 1963. She requested the department to inspect the jewellery to satisfy as to whether they were purchased in the year in question or were old so as to clear the doubt of the department regarding investment in year in question. The revenue, however, merely on the basis that the financial position of the assessee's father after two years of the assessee’s marriage was not sound, rejected the explanation of the assessee.
Held, that the authorities rejected the plea of the assessee regarding inspecting of the ornaments for determining whether they were old or new which could have helped in removing any possible doubts in the minds of the department. There was no evidence available on the file of the revenue to indicate that there had been any purchases by the assessee of jewellery in the relevant previous year. Merely for the reason that the price of gold had increased at the time of making of the assessment or at the time of hearing of the appeal should not be kept as a base for deciding any such investment as it would only result in a distorted picture, especially when there was no evidence available to indicate that the acquisition was in the relevant previous year of appeal. Addition was made without any basis and was, therefore, deleted.

IV. Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Unexplained expenditure (On-money) - Assessment years 2016-17, 2018-19 and 2023-24 - Pursuant to search, Assessing Officer alleged that assessee paid cash on-money for purchase of land at Halol and added 20 per cent of agreement value under section 69C - It was noted that addition rested solely on a general statement of Shri Rakesh Talati and certain WhatsApp communications - Statement lacked transaction-specific particulars regarding land, seller, amount, date or actual payment of cash, while WhatsApp chats pertained to a proposed Valsad transaction and not to Halol land purchases - Further, no seller confirmation, cash trail, seized material or other corroborative evidence was found and Assessing Officer adopted a uniform estimation of 20 per cent without any factual basis - Whether since foundational fact of actual expenditure itself remained unproved, estimation could not substitute evidence and addition under section 69C was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 102, 103 and 105] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 - Unexplained expenditure (Writ Jurisdiction) - Assessment year 2021-22 - Assessee had purchased huge quantum of bullion/jewellery from three sellers namely Shiv Sahai, Diamond and Surana for a sum of Rs. 234.15 crores - It had also paid commission to foreign and local agents for procuring buyers - Assessing Officer had disallowed aforesaid expenses and computed a sum of Rs. 240.18 crores as total income of petitioner for reason that petitioner could not produce any documentary proof to prove genuineness of said expenses - Assessee had filed a writ petition challenging order passed by Assessing Officer - It was observed that Surana was under liquidation and had sold jewellery to assessee pursuant to an auction conducted by Company Secretary appointed as Insolvency Resolution Professional - Assessee had attached sample invoice for a sum of Rs. 17.27 crores issued by Company Secretary, however, before Court it had filed copies of invoice for a sum of Rs. 127.35 crores - Further, although, during period dispute, movement of jewellery items including bullion were not required to accompany e-way bill in terms of rule 138(4)(a) of GST Rules, 2017, as amended by Notification No. 12/2018 - Central Tax with effect from 1-4-2018, assessee ought to have filed GST Returns of supplier and GST Returns in Form GST 2A - These documents were not furnished by assessee - And, issues regarding payment of commission to both Indian and foreign agents were not properly explained by assessee - Whether since there were several disputed question of facts which did not call for adjudication in a summary proceedings under article 226 of Constitution, writ was to be dismissed and assessee was to be given liberty to file a statutory appeals before Appellate Authority both against impugned assessment order - Held, yes [Paras 53 to 56] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where there were several disputed question of facts as regards commission paid by assessee to foreign and local agents for procuring buyers and expenditure incurred for purchase of bullion/jewellery which did not call for adjudication in a summary proceedings under article 226 of Constitution, writ petition filed by assessee was to be dismissed

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Cash deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee had made cash deposit during demonetization period in her bank account - Assessing Officer held that cash sales shown by assessee during period of 10 days just before demonetization was not genuine but fabricated and after thought being colourable device used to show unaccounted cash as accounted one - Thus, Assessing Officer made addition of said amount under section 68 - It was noted that Assessing Officer had accepted transactions about purchase and sale of jewellery in gold and silver without raising any doubt regarding books of account, purchase and sale stock registers and bills produced by assessee - Further, cash transaction before demonetization period was also revealed by assessee as period before demonetization was also period of Diwali and that itself showed that why cash transaction took place in that particular period - Whether since stock register as well as family evidences produced by assessee were found to be genuine and cash transaction had also been proved by assessee being genuine transaction, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Assessing Officer has clearly noted that the assessee had produced purchase vouchers for old jewellery and diamonds. He also noted that assessee was maintaining branch-wise accounts which were consolidated at its Head Office. It is also noted from the assessment order that assessee had filed details of various expenses incurred including TDS reconciliation. Admittedly, assessee was in the business of selling jewellery and it was also purchasing old gold and old diamonds from its customers, who wanted to exchange their old jewellery with new jewellery. • Contention of the assessee that it was not effecting any cash purchase from its customers, has not been effectively rebutted. Case of the assessee is that it was effecting purchase of old jewellery from customers who were willing to buy new jewellery from the assessee. In some of the cases, when old jewellery were given, they were taken for manufacturing new jewellery or to make certain customized changes required by customers. The view of the Assessing Officer that unless and until the sale and purchase were effected on same day, section 40A(3) was attracted cannot be accepted. [Para 12]

Applicability of rule 6DD of Income-tax Rules, 1962

• Thus, where the payments were effected to a customer on account of adjustment resulting out of an exchange of old jewellery with new jewellery, then it does get covered under the exception clause (d) of rule 6DD. [Para 13]

Violation of section 40A(3) in case of appearance of contra entries in cash book

• When in the cash book, assessee showed a purchase of jewellery for cash, the actual scenario was that it was only a credit purchase since there were contra entries in the cash book itself giving credit to concerned seller. At the time of effecting the sales, the entries were made in a reverse manner for adjusting against the credit. Such transactions could not be considered as violative of section 40A(3), just for a reason that contra entries appeared in the cash book. No doubt, assessee might have produced before Commissioner (Appeals) books of account, purchase vouchers and stock register. However, there is no violation of rule 46A for the reason that Assessing Officer has nowhere mentioned that assessee had failed to produce any records or books called for. Just because assessee could point out to Commissioner (Appeals), by producing the same cash book as produced before the Assessing Officer that there were no cash purchases whatsoever effected by it from its customers, will not be a reason to say that there was any violation of rule 46A. There is no case for the revenue that books produced by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) were different from the books produced by it before the Assessing Officer. [Para 13]

• In view of above, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the disallowance made under section 40A(3). [Para 15]

Insertion of new section 54C.

9. In the Income-tax Act, after section 54B, the following section shall be inserted with effect from the 1st day of April, 1973, namely: —

Capital gain on transfer of jewellery held for personal use not to be charged in certain cases.

'54C. Where the capital gain arises from the transfer of a capital asset, being jewellery held for personal use by the assessee or any member of his family dependent on him, and the assessee has, with-in a period of' six months after such transfer, acquired any other jewellery for personal use by the assessee or any member of his, family dependent on him, the capital gain shall be dealt with in accordance with the following provisions of this section, that is to say,—

(i) if the cost of the jewellery so acquired is not less than the full value of the consideration received or accruing in respect of the transferred jewellery, the whole of such capital gain shall not be charged under section 45; or

(ii) if the cost of the jewellery so acquired is less than the full value of the consideration received or accruing in respect of the transferred jewellery, so much of the capital gain as bears to the whole of the capital gain the same proportion as the cost of the jewellery so acquired bears to the full value of the consideration received or accruing in respect of the transferred jewellery shall not be charged under section 45.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "jewellery" shall have the same meaning as is assigned to it in the Explanation to sub clause (ii) of clause (14) section 2.'.

This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

■

It is not under dispute that the assessee has accounted the receipt as money received and deposited into the bank account directly by the party to whom the goods has been sold. This method of depositing the cash has regularly been followed by the assessee even in the past years and for an amount of Rs. 32,61,029/- is not disputed by the revenue.

■

The only dispute is of the SBN deposited into the bank account directly by the party for which even the assessee is not aware that how much legal tender deposited and how much SBN. Thus, the now the issue to be examined as to whether the assessee is under any obligation in such a situation as per the RBI circular or not, as the revenue while making the addition heavily relied upon the guidelines of the RBI and the relevant provisions thereof.

■

The Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017, defines 'appointed day' vide section 2(1)(a). As per section 2(1)(a) 'appointed day' means the 31st Day of December 2016. Section 5 of the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act 2017 also deals with prohibition on holding transferring or receiving specified bank notes. Section 5 states that 'on and from the appointed day, no person shall knowingly or voluntarily, hold, transfer or receive any specified bank note'.

■

Therefore, the SBN can be measured in monetary terms since the guarantee of the Central Government and the liability of Reserve Bank of India does not cease to exist till 31.12.2016. Thus, the assessee as per his regular practice has received directly into the bank account and the said money though not accepted directly by the assessee but the same has been deposited by the parties to whom the assessee has sold the goods.

■

The RBI has placed the restriction and taking the declaration as per the Annexure-5 from the person whose deposit the money and undisputedly this money has not been deposited by the assessee and therefore, furnishing at Annexure-5 by the assessee is out of question. It was the Assessing Officer who might have issued the section 133(6) to the respective party or to the bank and called for the details to justify the averments made by the assessee and thus, when the sales is not disputed and in fact the part of the cash in the demonetised period is not disputed the action of the lower authority in sustaining the addition under section 69A is incorrect and thus hereby directed to be deleted. In nutshell when the sales are not in dispute and found genuine and even for that part of the cash is considered as explained in the same demonetisation period which are not SBN out of the same sales merely the part of the other amount directly deposited into the bank account by the seller though SBN cannot be considered as unexplained money in the hands of the assessee as the same has not been received by the assessee directly and the same was received by the bank which was permitted till 31st December to be received by the bank. Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - FACT: The assessee voluntarily disclosed gold and diamonds jewellery under section 65(1) of VDIA 1997. The declaration as submitted by the assessee came to be accepted by the Commissioner and a certificate under section 68(2) of VDIS 1997 came to be issued.

Subsequently assessee filed return for relevant assessment year by declaring negative income from sale of above said VDIS declared gold and diamonds jewellery items, which had been converted into bullion after smelting and separating the diamonds through a goldsmith.

The Assessing Officer rejected the capital gains income from sale of VDIS declared items and entire sale consideration of the said items came to be charged to tax under section 68.

HELD: Findings of the authorities to reject the claim of assessee were on the ground that assessee had not examined any person from the above said jewellery firms to establish gold declared under VDIS had been smelted by him. It was also held that description of gold purity, diamond carat, colour and cut are not mentioned in the sale invoices. [Para 5]

It was, however, noticed that weight of the items sold was produced together with copies of bank drafts and payments receivd by the assessee on the said items. Yet, Assessing Officer did not accept the same. If at all, Assessing Officer was of the view that declaration made by the assessee is incorrect, on the premise that shops shown in the purchase invoice and sale bills, had not yet been occupied by the respective jewellers and have relied upon any other evidence, it was mandatory for the Assessing Officer to confront the said evidence to the assessees and after eliciting the say of assessees, he could have either rejected the same or accepted. However, such an exercise was not undertaken. But on the other hand, evidence which is said to have been collected during the course of enquiry, is sought to be used against assessees to disallow the claim without extending any opportunity to assessees to rebut the same. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that either the weight or gold sold by the assessees after smelting is different from the jewellery declared by the assessees in their declaration filed under section 65(1) of VDIS 1997. In fact, initial burden cash on the assessee has been discharged by establishing and proving that sold items were the items which had been declared by them under VDIS 1997. [Para 6]

In fact, Tribunal in its various decisions rendered in respect of the assessees who were similarly placed, who also contended that gold declared by them under VDIS had been smelted through had accepted assessee's explanation.[Para 8]

11.9 Interest under section 220(2)

Section 220(2) of the Act provides for a charge of interest for failure to pay any amount pursuant to the notice of demand under section 156 of the Act.

Section 200A of the Act provides for processing of TDS statements and recovery of tax including interest under section 201(1A) of the Act.

The above provisions may result into charge of interest twice in respect of the same amount. Finance Act, 2012 inserts sub-section (2B) in section 220, with effect from 1-7-2012, to provide that where interest is charged under section 201(1A) on the amount of tax specified in intimation issued under section 200A (1), for any period, then, no interest shall be charged under section 220(2) on the same amount for the same period.

11.10 Person responsible for paying

Section 204 of the Act, for the purpose of sections 190 to 203AA1 and section 285 gives meaning of 'person responsible for paying'. Memorandum explains that "There is a lack of clarity in the case of payment made by Central Government or by a State Government as to who is the person responsible for paying ".

In order to provide clarity, in section 204 (listing the person responsible for paying), Finance Act, 2012 inserts clause (iv) effective 1-7-2012.

For credit or payment of sum chargeable under the Act made by on or behalf of the said Governments, the person responsible for paying would be:

(a) the drawing and disbursing officer; or

(b) any other person, by whatever name called, responsible for crediting or paying such sum.

Section 206C obliges sellers of certain goods [listed in table below sub-section (1) including alcoholic liquor, tendu leaves, timber, scrap, etc.] to collect tax from a buyer at the rates specified in the table.

11.11-1 Amendment

To extend the scope thereof, Finance Act, 2012 carries out the following amendments, with effect from 1-7-2012, in the section :

(a) It would now also apply to:

(a) Sale of minerals, being coal or lignite or iron ore; and

(b) Sale of Bullion or jewellery.

(b) Consequential amendments pursuant to the widening of the scope.

(c) Goods utilised for power generation are not subject to tax collection.

(d) A proviso is inserted in sub-section (6A) to provide for the circumstances in which a person responsible for collecting tax may not be regarded as an assessee deemed to be in default, on the same lines as the first proviso to section 201(1). (see para 11.8.4)

(e) A proviso is inserted in sub-section (7) to provide for change of interest in case of Assessee not deemed to be in default.

11.11-2 Inclusion of specified minerals

Memorandum explains: "Mining sector is an important segment but the trading of minerals remained largely unregulated resulting in non-reporting or under- reporting of trading in minerals for the taxation purpose. In order to collect tax at the earliest point of time and also to improve reporting mechanism of transactions in mining sector tax at .. 1% shall be collected by the seller from the buyer of the following minerals: (a) Coal; (b) Lignite; and (c) Iron ore".

Having regard to the object, in the Table below sub-section (1) ('the Table') 'entry' (vii) is inserted to prescribe the nature of goods as 'minerals, being coal, lignite or iron ore' and the percentage, namely, 1%.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee had acquired certain pieces of diamond with cracks and spots during the assessment year 1975-76. Such diamonds were declared by the assessee under the VDIS, 1997. During the relevant assessment year, few of such diamonds were got processed and after processing, the finished diamonds were sold. For the purpose of computation of capital gain, the assessee opted for fair market value of diamonds as on 1-4-1981 on basis of valuation report of valuer for processed diamonds. The Assessing Officer did not accept the computation made by the assessee and he computed capital gain by applying cost of inflation index method in reverse direction, on value of diamond declared under the VDIS as on 1-4-1987 to determine fair market value of diamond on 1-4-1981. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal :

The immunity given by section 68 of the Finance Act, 1997 incorporating VDIS is limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery stands accepted and the amount credited in the books of the declarant to the extent of value of the jewellery so declared cannot be assessed as income of the declarant for any assessment year under any provision of the Income-tax Act including the provisions of section 68. This immunity, however, stops there and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further, either expressly or even by implication, to cover the sale of jewellery declared under VDIS also. The Assessing Officer is not only empowered to go into the genuineness of the transaction of sale of jewellery declared under VDIS, but he is duty-bound to do so in order to ensure that the scheme is not misused by the declarants for any more benefits than what are intended to be given under the scheme. It is, thus, open to the department to go into the genuineness of the transactions of sale of jewellery declared under VDIS and examine the same in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Income-tax Act. [Para 153]

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer treated the sale of jewellery as bogus mainly because firm 'B' did not respond to the letters/summons issued by him and the Inspector deputed to visit the said concern could not trace it at the address given. [Para 164]

The facts clearly showed that the matter regarding genuineness of transactions of purchase and sale of jewellery by firm B was still under investigation by the department. The issue relating to genuineness of the transactions of purchase and sale of jewellery in the cases of firm 'B' had been investigated in detail and the decision thereon had a direct bearing on the ultimate fate of the case of the assessee-HUF. Accordingly, the appeals filed in the case of the firm had already been disposed of holding that the assessment made under section 158BC, read with section 158BD in the case of firm B was bad in law. On merit, following conclusion drawn in the case of company Bemco which was an associate concern of firm 'B' as well as its partners, the transaction relating to sale of jewellery in the case of the assessee was genuine. Accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 68 was deleted. [Paras 165 and 166]

The Assessing Officer further noted that, the assessee has furnished VAT returns belatedly to cover up the backdated sale bills issued to the customers to show sufficient cash balance in the books of account to explain cash deposits into the bank account. It is also not in dispute that, the assessee was having sufficient stock-in-hand to explain the sale bills issued to the customers between 1-11-2016 to 8-11-2016. The sales declared by the assessee are recorded in the books of account and also part of the turnover declared for the year under consideration which suffered taxation. Once the assessee has recorded sales in the books of account, which is supported by necessary sales bills with a corresponding stock-in-hand, the Assessing Officer ought not to have made additions towards cash deposits as unexplained money only on the ground that, there is abnormal variation in cash sales during the demonetization period when compared to earlier or subsequent periods. It was a well-known fact during the demonetization period that, there was a mad rush in jewellery shops for purchasing gold jewellery out of demonetized currency when the demonetization was announced on 8-11-2016. In the instant case, going by the facts available on record, the assessee has reported major sales on 7-11-2016, which is the previous day of the demonetization was announced, and from the details furnished by the assessee, it is very clear that, the assessee has made sales of gold jewellery in cash which is the source for cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period on 14-11-2016. Since the cash deposited into the bank account is supported by necessary cash balance available as per books of account maintained by the assessee which was further supported by necessary sales bills, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer to make addition towards cash deposits under section 69A as unexplained money cannot be sustained. Although the Assessing Officer has disbelieved the sales on the basis of VAT returns submitted by the assessee for the month of November, 2016 and claimed that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover backdated sales, but going by the history of the assessee in filing the VAT returns, it is evident that, for all the months in the financial year 2016-17, the assessee has filed VAT returns belatedly and from the above, it is very clear that, the argument of the Assessing Officer that, the assessee has filed belated VAT returns to cover up backdated sales, is contrary to the evidence available on record and cannot be accepted. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has erred in making addition towards cash deposit into the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A. Thus, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition made under section 69A. [Para 20]

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus

12.12

Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

12.12-1 Evidence for ascertaining the value of investments

During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee. Assessee submitted a bill in respect of purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges. However, AO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee. Held once the identity of the diamond jewellery found during the course of search had been accepted as explainable from the purchase voucher and labour charges bill produced by the assessee at the time of search as well as during the course of regular assessment proceedings, the addition of the difference could be made by the AO only by establishing the fact that the value stated in the purchase invoice was fictitious. The burden clearly lay upon the department to prove that the value shown in the purchase invoice was not the real value. The department had not brought any material whatever on records to prove that the value of such diamonds embedded in the diamond jewellery at the time of its purchase in the month of July 1981 was understated in the purchase invoices. Such a burden was required to be discharged by the department by bringing clinching and conclusive evidence on record. The AO had not even examined the jeweller from whom these diamonds were purchased. The assessee had successfully discharged the initial burden of proving the source of acquisition of aforesaid diamond jewellery by producing the aforesaid bills at the time of search. The AO had completely failed to bring any evidence on record to show that the cost of ornaments shown by the assessee did not represent the real cost. Therefore, the addition on account of the difference in value of diamond ornaments in question is not justified and deserves to be deleted. - Gautam Laljibhai Gajjar v. ITO [1991] 37 ITD 514 (Ahd.)

Where Revenue had made additions under section 69 on basis of photocopies of documents, statements and oath given by a foreigner, such additions could not be sustained unless assessee had been given an opportunity either to see original documents or even to cross-examine party in whose books of account these entries were made. - P.V. Jewellers v. ITO [1993] 45 TTJ (Jp.) 541

Where Assessing Officer had made certain additions to assessee's income on basis of enquiries made from Excise Department and other manufacturers which were not intimated to assessee to enable it advance its view, additions so made were not justified. - Dy. CIT v. Hari Chand Sri Gopal [1994] 48 TTJ (Delhi) 151

Where discrepancy in the figure mentioned in the transfer memos was attributable to clerical errors and did not represent physical transfer of cash, addition on account of such discrepancy was not justified. - Sadhoo Beedi Depot v. Dy. CIT [1995] 51 TTJ (Coch.) 550

Where while considering source of alleged unexplained investment, AO had not taken into account certain unutilised withdrawals by assessee from bank, additions on account of unexplained investment were not justified. - P. K. Narayanan v. Asstt. CIT [1995] 53 TTJ (Coch.) 181

INCOME TAX: Where AO made addition for unexplained cash purchases in diamond trading business solely based on third-party software recovered from search on another entity without providing corroborative material or opportunity for cross-examination to assessee who maintained proper books and banking records, such addition under section 69C could not be sustained.

The partner of the assessee firm. 'M', in his statements made before the investigation wing, had stated that the sales had been made in cash and the persons, through whom sales were made, were unverifiable. In fact, he said that he knew the names of the customers to whom sales had been made, personally but he did not disclose the names due to professional/trade secret. It was in clear contradiction to his first statement recorded on 6-5-1999, when he stated that he did not know any such person and the buyers approached him directly. It was, thus, a case where the partner in the assessee-firm had been changing his stand as regards the particulars of sales. No evidence worth any credence had been led either in the course of the assessment proceedings or appellate proceedings to establish that the sales had been made and the cash deposited in the bank account was in lieu of the sales made of jewellery. In fact, unverifiability of the sales had been accepted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, when he had enhanced the income returned and the assessee, in the impugned proceedings, had not challenged that finding. Mere furnishing of cash memos could not by any stretch of imagination, be made a sole basis to conclude that any sales had been made by the assessee. Thus, the sales made by the assessee were unverifiable and unacceptable. Moreover, the entire transaction of purchase and sale of jewellery had been carried out by the assessee in a particular manner and abnormal circumstances, which irrefutably led to a conclusion that there was no business per se of the assessee of purchase and sale of jewellery. The assessee-firm did not even had the necessary infrastructure, i.e., dharam kanta to carry on the business of purchase and sale of diamond jewellery, which is the most essential infrastructure. Even otherwise, no particulars had been placed on record to show that such jewellery was allegedly purchased and sold by the assessee with a weighing scale of a third party. In fact, the evidence furnished by the assessee in the shape of purchase bills and sales bills did not include the weighment slips, which, as per the admission of the assessee, were the fundamental requirements for any transaction of purchase/sale of jewellery. There were no employees of the firm other than one 'G', who had not been produced in the course of the assessment proceedings and even his particulars had not been made available at any stage. Even as regards to his purported duties, there was a contradiction. In the initial statement, 'M' stated that said employee's duty was to assist him in carrying the cash to the bank, whereas subsequently even the same was contradicted by stating that when he went to deposit the cash, he stayed back at the premises. Thus, it was not possible to accept that the assessee had employed any such person. Even otherwise, it was not possible to carry on business of such a huge magnitude with only one employee and that too, having no formal qualifications. It had been stated by 'M' before the investigation wing and the Assessing Officer that the business was carried on with minimum furniture of one table, two chairs and a half size almirah, which was also used as a safe. However, it appeared that even the infrastructure as contended by the assessee in the shape of almirah, one table and two chairs was not available with the assessee to carry on the business of the projected magnitude. Further, there was no past track record of the assessee-firm. It had allegedly carried on the operations of business only for a short period of time and even within that short period of time, the entire alleged purchases of jewellery were from the persons, who had furnished declarations under the VDIS, 1997, and for all such purchases the sales were only in cash. In fact, even independently, the purchases had not been proved by the assessee-firm. Mere issue of purchase bills could not be regarded as sufficient basis to hold that the jewellery had been purchased by the assessee-firm. In that connection, the statements of four persons had been recorded by the investigation wing, wherein all of them had confirmed that they had not sold any jewellery to the assessee. Though in the assessment proceedings, they had retracted from their original statements, yet such retraction was not supported by any adequate reason. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act. That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further
