On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ In any given case, whether the sales claimed by the assessee are genuine or not, is a question of fact and the answer will depend on specific facts and circumstances of the case. In the present case, the addition has been made, disbelieving the assessee's claim that cash sales in SBNs were made, amounting to Rs. 9.25 crores on 8-11-2016. The case of revenue rests essentially on hypothesis that it was unlikely, based on materials available on record, surrounding circumstances, human conduct, preponderance of probabilities and nature of incriminating information/evidence available on record, that cash sales amounting to aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores were made in SBNs on 8-11-2016. No specific transaction of sale, not even one, has been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue. In fact the Assessing Officer himself has treated sale amounting to Rs. 75.99 lakhs (made in SBNs) to be genuine but has disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.25 crores. In the absence of any direct evidence to show that any specific sale transaction was not genuine or untrue, the question of fact before us is whether in the given facts and circumstances it is possible that the assessee might have made sale of aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores in cash on 8-11-2016. It is quite understandable, that after announcement of demonetization, the people in possession of SBNs were desperate to use it for purchase of gold, diamond and silver jewellery and other items before the deadline after which SBNs could not have been used. In such a desperate situation, it is quite understandable that customers would not exercise choice in selection as they might have done in normal course. Therefore, the submissions made from assessee's side that the customers instantly purchased whatever they saw on the counter, using SBNs, is acceptable. Further it is quite understandable that the assessee brought additional manpower to deal with and to attend to the extraordinary rush of customers. Therefore, the submission made from the assessee's side that family members, relatives, friends and staff of other business entities were utilized to attend the extraordinary rush of customers is also acceptable. It is not in dispute that the aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.25 crores included sale amounting to Rs. 1.67 crores which attracted penalty under section 271DA for contravention of section 269ST. Further it is not in dispute that the aforesaid total sales of Rs. 1.67 crores (consisting of each transaction exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs in cash) were not made through serially numbered sales vouchers. Instead, these transactions were interspersed with other sale transactions in cash, below Rs. 2 lakhs. These facts clearly establish that the sales claimed by the assessee to have been made in cash were genuine. Moreover, the contention that if the assessee had any intention to book bogus sales, then the assessee would not have booked sales inviting penalty under section 271BA is a reasonable one. It is further seen that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the assessee's books of account. Moreover, the assessee has shown the sales in VAT returns, which have been accepted by VAT authorities. It is not in dispute that the assessee had sufficient stock in trade to make sale as claimed, on 8-11-2016. Revenue has not doubted the purchases made by the assessee. Further not even a single specific sale transaction has been proved to be fake, bogus or untrue.

HELD: ■

The entire case of the revenue is built upon the basis of suspicion regarding the sales booked by the assessee prior to the start of demonetization period. The Assessing Officer has rejected the books of account merely because there was a spike in cash advances on three dates. However, the comparative data furnished by the assessee clearly dispels this suspicion. A perusal of the chart reveals that the cash sales in the year under consideration were in fact significantly lower than the preceding year. When the assessee has demonstrated that in the previous year, during the corresponding period, the cash sales were much higher, the allegation of ‘abnormal’ sales during the demonetization period falls flat. The data furnished by the assessee shows that the assessee’s total sales as well as cash sales during the year under consideration including the relevant demonetization period were comparatively very less than the preceding financial year. This data shows that the assessee’s cash sales were not abnormal during the relevant period and Assessing Officer’s suspicion of cash sales is not based on any reliable material. [Para 11]

■

Further, the Assessing Officer has not pointed out any discrepancy in the stock register, and the assessee was evidently possessed of the requisite stock to effect the impugned sales. It is a matter of record that the purchases have been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income. The notices issued under section 133(6) were largely complied with, and the mere fact that one party went into bankruptcy does not make the entire purchases bogus. Though the Assessing Officer has doubted the purchases, it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had not debited the amount of purchases from its books or that the assessee had made purchases out of its unexplained income. Once the purchases are accepted and the stock is not disputed, the sales flowing out of such stock cannot be treated as non-genuine. The sales have been recorded in the books of account and the profit arising therefrom has been offered to tax. Therefore, the entire receipts from the corresponding sales cannot be treated as unaccounted income of the assessee; only the profit element embedded in such sales can be taxed, which the assessee has duly offered for taxation. Taxing the gross receipts again under section 68 would amount to double taxation of the same amount. [Para 12]

This raises serious doubts about the genuineness of confirmation because in the normal circumstances confirmation is sought from the party only when it is required by the other party during the course of assessment or other proceedings. In the present case, it appears that this confirmation was obtained by the appellant much before the date of query raised by the Assessing Officer which indicates a prior planning and pre-mediated approach. This raises serious doubts about the genuineness of the confirmation filed and in my opinion, this confirmation could not be said to be sufficient to discharge the onus of proving the sale of jewellery in the context of the following facts:—

(i )

Though the appellant claimed jewellery to be very old and having sentimental value, the appellant had promptly sold this very jewellery immediately after the date of receipt of VDIS certificate.

(ii)

Jewellery was sold to unknown party of Delhi i.e., M/s. Bishan Chand Mukesh Kumar claimed to have been introduced through a relative of the appellant to whom the appellant was not able to identify.

(iii)

The appellant handed over jewellery worth Rs.14 lakhs to this unknown jeweller of Delhi without receiving any payment on the delivery of the jewellery.

Although confirmation has been received by the Assessing Officer, but the party is not traceable at the address given on the confirmation.

(v)

All the letters sent by the Assessing Officer through registered post/speed post have not been received back undelivered.

The said party i.e., M/s. Bishan Chand Mukesh Kumar, Delhi is stated to be not traceable as per the report of the Inspector, referred to above.

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. ■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. The partner of the assessee firm. 'M', in his statements made before the investigation wing, had stated that the sales had been made in cash and the persons, through whom sales were made, were unverifiable. In fact, he said that he knew the names of the customers to whom sales had been made, personally but he did not disclose the names due to professional/trade secret. It was in clear contradiction to his first statement recorded on 6-5-1999, when he stated that he did not know any such person and the buyers approached him directly. It was, thus, a case where the partner in the assessee-firm had been changing his stand as regards the particulars of sales. No evidence worth any credence had been led either in the course of the assessment proceedings or appellate proceedings to establish that the sales had been made and the cash deposited in the bank account was in lieu of the sales made of jewellery. In fact, unverifiability of the sales had been accepted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order, when he had enhanced the income returned and the assessee, in the impugned proceedings, had not challenged that finding. Mere furnishing of cash memos could not by any stretch of imagination, be made a sole basis to conclude that any sales had been made by the assessee. Thus, the sales made by the assessee were unverifiable and unacceptable. Moreover, the entire transaction of purchase and sale of jewellery had been carried out by the assessee in a particular manner and abnormal circumstances, which irrefutably led to a conclusion that there was no business per se of the assessee of purchase and sale of jewellery. The assessee-firm did not even had the necessary infrastructure, i.e., dharam kanta to carry on the business of purchase and sale of diamond jewellery, which is the most essential infrastructure. Even otherwise, no particulars had been placed on record to show that such jewellery was allegedly purchased and sold by the assessee with a weighing scale of a third party. In fact, the evidence furnished by the assessee in the shape of purchase bills and sales bills did not include the weighment slips, which, as per the admission of the assessee, were the fundamental requirements for any transaction of purchase/sale of jewellery. There were no employees of the firm other than one 'G', who had not been produced in the course of the assessment proceedings and even his particulars had not been made available at any stage. Even as regards to his purported duties, there was a contradiction. In the initial statement, 'M' stated that said employee's duty was to assist him in carrying the cash to the bank, whereas subsequently even the same was contradicted by stating that when he went to deposit the cash, he stayed back at the premises. Thus, it was not possible to accept that the assessee had employed any such person. Even otherwise, it was not possible to carry on business of such a huge magnitude with only one employee and that too, having no formal qualifications. It had been stated by 'M' before the investigation wing and the Assessing Officer that the business was carried on with minimum furniture of one table, two chairs and a half size almirah, which was also used as a safe. However, it appeared that even the infrastructure as contended by the assessee in the shape of almirah, one table and two chairs was not available with the assessee to carry on the business of the projected magnitude. Further, there was no past track record of the assessee-firm. It had allegedly carried on the operations of business only for a short period of time and even within that short period of time, the entire alleged purchases of jewellery were from the persons, who had furnished declarations under the VDIS, 1997, and for all such purchases the sales were only in cash. In fact, even independently, the purchases had not been proved by the assessee-firm. Mere issue of purchase bills could not be regarded as sufficient basis to hold that the jewellery had been purchased by the assessee-firm. In that connection, the statements of four persons had been recorded by the investigation wing, wherein all of them had confirmed that they had not sold any jewellery to the assessee. Though in the assessment proceedings, they had retracted from their original statements, yet such retraction was not supported by any adequate reason. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act. That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further

Section 206C

Finance Act, 2013

13.3 Tax Collected at Source - Section 206C

13.3-1 Existing Provisions

In order to reduce the quantum of cash transaction in bullion and jewellery sector and for curbing the flow of unaccounted money in the trading system of bullion and jewellery, the Finance Act, 2012 inserted new sub-section (1D) in section 206C with effect from 1-7-2012 to provide for TCS on cash sale of jewellery and bullion to be collected by the seller.

According to new sub-section (1D), every person, being a seller, who receives any amount in cash as consideration for sale of bullion (excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less) or jewellery, shall, at the time of receipt of such amount in cash, collect from the buyer, a sum equal to 1% of sale consideration as income-tax, if such consideration,—

(i)

for bullion, exceeds two hundred thousand rupees; or

(ii)

for jewellery, exceeds five hundred thousand rupees.

13.3-2 Amendments

The Finance Act, 2013 has omitted the words "(excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less)" with effect from 1-6-2013.

13.3-3 Impact

So cash sale of gold coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less will also attract TCS with effect from 1-6-2013 if consideration exceeds Rs. 2,00,000.

To put in other words, with effect from June 1, 2013, consideration of "any coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less" shall not be excluded while calculating the monetary limit of Rs. 2,00,000.

Press release dated 1-5-2013 read as under :—

Currently, sale in cash of bullion (excluding coin or any other article weighing 10 grams or less) in excess of Rs. 2 lakh or jewellery in excess of Rs. 5 lakh is subject to Tax Collection at Source (TCS) @ 1%. As coins were neither included in bullion nor in jewellery, therefore, coins, even when amounting to more than Rs. 2 lakh in value, were being sold in cash without TCS.

The Finance Bill, 2013 proposes to delete exclusion of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less from bullion. Hence, the sale of bullion (including coins/articles) in cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%. Similarly, sale of jewellery in cash in excess of Rs. 5 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%.

It is not a new levy of tax but continuation of old levy except withdrawal of exemption in the case of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less.

In any given case, whether the sales claimed by the assessee are genuine or not, is a question of fact and the answer will depend on specific facts and circumstances of the case. In the present case, the addition has been made, disbelieving the assessee's claim that cash sales in SBNs were made, amounting to Rs. 9.25 crores on 8-11-2016. The case of revenue rests essentially on hypothesis that it was unlikely, based on materials available on record, surrounding circumstances, human conduct, preponderance of probabilities and nature of incriminating information/evidence available on record, that cash sales amounting to aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores were made in SBNs on 8-11-2016. No specific transaction of sale, not even one, has been proved by revenue, with supporting evidence, to be bogus or untrue. In fact the Assessing Officer himself has treated sale amounting to Rs. 75.99 lakhs (made in SBNs) to be genuine but has disbelieved the remaining amount of Rs. 9.25 crores. In the absence of any direct evidence to show that any specific sale transaction was not genuine or untrue, the question of fact before us is whether in the given facts and circumstances it is possible that the assessee might have made sale of aforesaid amount of Rs. 9.25 crores in cash on 8-11-2016. It is quite understandable, that after announcement of demonetization, the people in possession of SBNs were desperate to use it for purchase of gold, diamond and silver jewellery and other items before the deadline after which SBNs could not have been used. In such a desperate situation, it is quite understandable that customers would not exercise choice in selection as they might have done in normal course. Therefore, the submissions made from assessee's side that the customers instantly purchased whatever they saw on the counter, using SBNs, is acceptable. Further it is quite understandable that the assessee brought additional manpower to deal with and to attend to the extraordinary rush of customers. Therefore, the submission made from the assessee's side that family members, relatives, friends and staff of other business entities were utilized to attend the extraordinary rush of customers is also acceptable. It is not in dispute that the aforesaid sale of Rs. 9.25 crores included sale amounting to Rs. 1.67 crores which attracted penalty under section 271DA for contravention of section 269ST. Further it is not in dispute that the aforesaid total sales of Rs. 1.67 crores (consisting of each transaction exceeding Rs. 2 lakhs in cash) were not made through serially numbered sales vouchers. Instead, these transactions were interspersed with other sale transactions in cash, below Rs. 2 lakhs. These facts clearly establish that the sales claimed by the assessee to have been made in cash were genuine. Moreover, the contention that if the assessee had any intention to book bogus sales, then the assessee would not have booked sales inviting penalty under section 271BA is a reasonable one. It is further seen that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the assessee's books of account. Moreover, the assessee has shown the sales in VAT returns, which have been accepted by VAT authorities. It is not in dispute that the assessee had sufficient stock in trade to make sale as claimed, on 8-11-2016. Revenue has not doubted the purchases made by the assessee. Further not even a single specific sale transaction has been proved to be fake, bogus or untrue.

According to new sub-section (1D), every person, being a seller, who receives any amount in cash as consideration for sale of bullion (excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less) or jewellery, shall, at the time of receipt of such amount in cash, collect from the buyer, a sum equal to 1% of sale consideration as income-tax, if such consideration,—

(i)

for bullion, exceeds two hundred thousand rupees; or

(ii) for jewellery, exceeds five hundred thousand rupees.

13.3-2 Amendments

The Finance Act, 2013 has omitted the words "(excluding any coin or any other article weighing ten grams or less)" with effect from 1-6-2013.

13.3-3 Impact

So cash sale of gold coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less will also attract TCS with effect from 1-6-2013 if consideration exceeds Rs. 2,00,000.

To put in other words, with effect from June 1, 2013, consideration of "any coin or any other article weighing 10 gms. or less" shall not be excluded while calculating the monetary limit of Rs. 2,00,000.

Press release dated 1-5-2013 read as under :—

Currently, sale in cash of bullion (excluding coin or any other article weighing 10 grams or less) in excess of Rs. 2 lakh or jewellery in excess of Rs. 5 lakh is subject to Tax Collection at Source (TCS) @ 1%. As coins were neither included in bullion nor in jewellery, therefore, coins, even when amounting to more than Rs. 2 lakh in value, were being sold in cash without TCS.

The Finance Bill, 2013 proposes to delete exclusion of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less from bullion. Hence, the sale of bullion (including coins/articles) in cash in excess of Rs. 2 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%. Similarly, sale of jewellery in cash in excess of Rs. 5 lakh shall be subject to TCS @1%.

It is not a new levy of tax but continuation of old levy except withdrawal of exemption in the case of coins/articles weighing 10 grams or less.

Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

12.12-1 Evidence for ascertaining the value of investments

During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee. Assessee submitted a bill in respect of purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges. However, AO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee. Held once the identity of the diamond jewellery found during the course of search had been accepted as explainable from the purchase voucher and labour charges bill produced by the assessee at the time of search as well as during the course of regular assessment proceedings, the addition of the difference could be made by the AO only by establishing the fact that the value stated in the purchase invoice was fictitious. The burden clearly lay upon the department to prove that the value shown in the purchase invoice was not the real value. The department had not brought any material whatever on records to prove that the value of such diamonds embedded in the diamond jewellery at the time of its purchase in the month of July 1981 was understated in the purchase invoices. Such a burden was required to be discharged by the department by bringing clinching and conclusive evidence on record. The AO had not even examined the jeweller from whom these diamonds were purchased. The assessee had successfully discharged the initial burden of proving the source of acquisition of aforesaid diamond jewellery by producing the aforesaid bills at the time of search. The AO had completely failed to bring any evidence on record to show that the cost of ornaments shown by the assessee did not represent the real cost. Therefore, the addition on account of the difference in value of diamond ornaments in question is not justified and deserves to be deleted. - Gautam Laljibhai Gajjar v. ITO [1991] 37 ITD 514 (Ahd.)

Jewellers v. ITO [1993] 45 TTJ (Jp.) 541

HELD: ■ The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

With respect to one-to-one mapping therefore only criteria is the sale of carats of the diamond. Assessee has shown that number of carats purchased from the three entities is 585.88 carats and the sale of the diamond is also 585.88 carats. The amount of purchases recorded is 6.27 crores whereas the sale of the same diamond is shown at 6.71 crores. With respect to purchases from RA Distributors Private Limited, the assessee has purchased 496.88 carats and identical carats were sold. The purchase price of these diamonds is Rs. 5.39 crores and the sale is Rs. 5.79 crores. With respect to the purchases from three different entities the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that assessee has purchased from these parties Rs. 5.29 crores, 6.97 crores and Rs. 7.40 crores out of which the Assessing Officer has doubted only Rs. 2.49 crore, 2.19 crores and Rs. 1.58 crores. The total purchases affected by the parties are also having identical billing narration. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly decided that there is a one-to-one mapping available from purchases which are considered as alleged bogus purchases by the Assessing Officer and corresponding sales. Further, it has been held that there is no connection established by the Assessing Officer with respect to purchases from these three parties by the assessee with the alleged bogus purchases recorded in the investigation wing information as well as the charge sheet filed by the enforcement directorate. The Assessing Officer has also not challenged that assessee has not maintain proper books of account including purchase and register, since register, stock register and day-to-day bank book. No specific defect or irregularity was recorded by the Assessing Officer. With respect to the gross profit computed by the assessee from bogus sales is based on the number of carats purchased by the assessee and the same number of carats sold by the assessee. With respect to purchases from three different entities, the Commissioner (Appeals) has computed gross profit of Rs. 44.49 Lacs and purchases from 'R' gross profit is computed at Rs. 40.72 lakhs. Thus, the average gross profit earned by the assessee on total purchases of Rs. 11.66 crores; assessee has earned gross profit of Rs. 85.21 lakhs, which is 6.81 per cent. Gross profit as per the regular books of account is 6.73 per cent. Thus, no infirmity can be found in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) whereas assessee has shown higher gross profit from alleged bogus purchases compared to its regular transaction. [Para 22]

In case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be the sufficient compliance; therefore, the assessee cannot be further burdened to show the colour and number of diamonds. When bills of purchases from other parties and from the same parties where part of the purchase consideration is accepted as genuine, no such details are available in the sale bill, there was no reason to deviate from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals).[Para 23]

If the alleged bogus purchases show gross profit higher than the regular gross profit shown by the assessee, no further addition is required to be made in the hands of the assessee. The logic behind this is that sale is already accounted for on the credit side of the profit and loss account. If the purchases are to be removed, the corresponding sale is also required to be removed from the profit and loss account, sales is higher than the purchases in rupees terms, therefore, the addition would be only required to be made to the extent of lower gross profit on alleged bogus purchases then the regular gross profit. This also takes the care of the argument that no proof of delivery of goods purchased are shown by the assessee, similarly, the sales are also bogus. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that amount invested in acquiring the bogus purchases should also be considered as an addition, because the only addition is disallowance of bogus purchases, no further addition is warranted. In view of this, the ground of appeal of the Assessing Officer are dismissed. [Para 24]

Admittedly, the assessee had neither made any disclosure of diamonds under the VDIS nor he had sold any diamond. The disclosure and the sale was made by the family members who had declared the same in their regular returns filed before search. The VDIS declaration by the family members had been accepted and certificate under section 68(2) of the Finance Act, 1997, had been issued by the Commissioner. The proprietor of the concern, who purchased the diamonds was examined by the Assessing Officer who accepted the purchases made by him from the family members. In search no incriminating material was found to hold that the sale was bogus. The statement of the family members heavily relied on by the Assessing Officer could not be a basis for drawing an adverse inference in view of the retraction of these statements and the affidavits of the family members filed before the Assessing Officer which remained uncontroverted. The sale proceeds were received by the family members and credited in their respective bank account. From these bank accounts, the assessee received the loan which was duly reflected in the regular returns. Thus, in the hands of the assessee the credit was fully explained. In these circumstances, the addition could not be made in the hands of the assessee.

In view of the above, the declaration made under VDIS and the sale of diamonds declared therein could not be held to be bogus/non-existent as held by the Assessing Officer. The addition made in the assessee’s hands, was, therefore, rightly deleted by the Commissioner (Appeals).

Based on information/material found during the search and seizure/ survey operations in case of partners of assessee-firm the departmental authorities observed that large amount of cash was deposited in various bank accounts of different entities, which, after layering were transferred to the assessee. The Assessing Officer found that as per the investigation carried out by the Investigation Wing, the assessee had purportedly sold gold and bullions to 44 entities controlled and managed by an entry operator, namely, Sonu Punjabi, which were sham transactions carried out during the demonetization period. It was alleged by the Assessing Officer that though notices under section 133(6) as well as summons under section 131 were issued, no information came from such entities as most of the summons returned back unserved. The Assessing Officer finally concluded that sales of gold/bullion to 44 entities allegedly controlled by Sonu Punjabi, were bogus sales and made for the purpose of introducing own money routed through bogus firms to its accounts. Thus, he treated the amount credited to the books of account as receipts from sale of gold/bullion, as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

The Assessing Officer further observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of gold/bullion worth Rs. 20.87 crore to RBPL and that in course of search and seizure operation conducted in case of M of RBPL statement under section 132(4) was recorded wherein he allegedly stated that cash amounting to Rs. 32.81 crore given to him by a firm, namely, DL Jewellers was deposited in the bank account of RBPL, for the purpose of transferring the fund to specific accounts on commission basis. The Assessing Officer ultimately concluded that the purported sales of gold/bullion to RBPL was bogus. Accordingly, he treated the receipt from sale of gold/bullion to RBPL as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee.

■

Further, the Assessing Officer observed that in the year under consideration the assessee had recorded sales of Rs. 19.30 lakhs to Olivia, towards sale of gold/ bullion. He observed that in course of survey conducted in the case of Olivia, it was found that the said company was incorporated in January 2015 and in assessment year 2015-16 it had filed the return of income offering NIL income without any turnover whereas, huge amount of cash was found to have been deposited in the bank account of Olivia, which suggested that the entity was an entry provider. Accordingly, he treated the amount in dispute as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE and added back to the income of the assessee. Similarly, he treated receipts from S.S Overseas as bogus sales and held it as unexplained cash credit under section 68 read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

On appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member, having found that the assessee was able to establish the identity and creditworthiness of the entities purchasing gold/bullion from the assessee as well as the genuineness of the transactions, held that not only the sales were genuine but none of the conditions of section 68 were applicable to the subject transactions. Accordingly, he deleted the entire addition. Whereas, the Judicial Member did not agree with the view expressed by the Accountant Member. He was of the view that not only the sales were bogus but the amount representing bogus sales was required to be added to the business income by treating them as unexplained investment under section 69. 10.8 Collection of tax at source [Section 206C]

Hitherto, sub-section (1D) provided that every person being seller who receives the sales consideration in cash on sale of bullion or jewellery, in excess of certain amount, shall collect tax @ 1% from the buyer.

10.8-1 Amendments

Finance Act, 2016, with effect from 1-6-2016, has made the following amendments in section 206C of the Act :

In order to curb the cash transaction and bring unaccounted cash in the tax net, it has amended sub-section (1D) to provide that sale of any goods or any services will also be subject to TCS provisions, if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a)

Consideration for goods or services exceeds Rs. 2,00,000.

(b)

Out of such consideration, any amount is received in cash (see para 10.8-3).

It has inserted a new proviso under sub-section (1D) as follows :

"Provided that no tax shall be collected at source under this sub-section on any amount on which tax has been deducted by the payer under Chapter XVII-B" (see para 10.8-3a)

It has inserted new sub-section (1E) as follows :

"Nothing contained in sub-section (1D) in relation to sale of any goods (other than bullion or jewellery) or providing any service shall apply to such class of buyers who fulfil such conditions, as may be prescribed."; (see para 10.8-4)

Sub-section (1F) is inserted to provide that sale of motor vehicle of the value exceeding Rs. 10 lakhs will also require collection of tax at source at 1% (see para 10.8-2);

It has made the consequential amendment in the definition of 'buyer' under Explanation (aa) to include purchaser of a motor vehicle and 'seller' under Explanation (c) so as to include an individual and HUF being the service provider (see para 10.8-5).

10.8-2 Sale of Motor Vehicle [Sub-section (1F)]

In terms of the amendment, if the value of motor vehicle exceeds Rs. 10,00,000, the seller will collect tax @ 1% of the value of such motor vehicle at the time of receipt of such amount from the buyer.

The transaction may be in cash or by the issue of a cheque or draft or by any other mode.

10.8-2a "Motor Vehicle" - Connotation of - 'Motor vehicle' has not been defined specifically under the Act. However, it is defined under section 2(28) of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 which reads as under :

'"motor vehicle" or "vehicle" means any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads whether the power of propulsion is transmitted thereto from an external or internal source and includes a chassis to which a body has not been attached and a trailer; but does not include a vehicle running upon fixed rails or a vehicle of a special type adapted for use only in a factory or in any other enclosed premises or a vehicle having less than four wheels fitted with engine capacity of not exceeding thirty five cubic centimetres."'

The above definition is only for the purpose of Motor Vehicle Act. Therefore, such meaning cannot be extended to the Income-tax law. Even Supreme Court in case of Assistant Commissioner (Anti-Evasion-I) v. Swaraj Mazda Ltd. [2001] 121 STC 255 held that in absence of the definition of the words 'motor vehicles' in the Sales-tax Act, the meaning given to 'motor vehicles' in the Motor Vehicle Act cannot be given to the said expression occurring in the Sales-tax Act or in the Notification issued thereunder.

11.11.5 Interest under section 206C(7)

Section 206C(7) provides for payment of simple interest in case of failure to collect whole or any part of tax, or after collecting payment thereof, by a person responsible for collecting tax.

Finance Act, 2012 inserts first proviso in section 206C(6A) (see para 11.8.4) to provide that in the circumstances specified therein the person shall not be deemed to be Assessee in default.

To charge the interest under sub-section (7) even in case of Assessee not deemed to be default, Finance Act, 2012 inserts a proviso in sub-section (7), effective 1-7-2012.

It provides that a person not deemed to be an assessee in default under the first proviso to sub-section (6A), who has failed to collect whole or any part of tax on any amount collected, would be liable to pay interest from the date on which the tax was collectible to the date of furnishing of return of income by a buyer etc.

To illustrate, the person was obliged to collect tax, say, on January 1. The buyer, etc., furnishes the return of income on July 31. The amount not collected by way of tax, say, is, say, Rs. 10,000. The person would be liable to pay interest on Rs. 10,000 for the period January 1 to July 31.

After perusing the orders of the lower authorities along with other materials placed on record, it was found that there was no infirmity in the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals). The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering the order of the Assessing Officer in the light of submissions made before him and other materials on record had found that there was lot of discrepancies and contradictions in the facts of the case and the statements recorded under section 132(4) in the case of ‘G’.

Further the Commissioner (Appeals) had taken into consideration the fact that there was no dispute that the assessee was having jewellery and diamonds, as the same were declared before the department while filing returns under VDIS. It was further noted by the Commissioner (Appeals) that the statement of ‘G’ was not provided to the assessee for filing her explanations/objections. Then a conclusion was arrived at by the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Assessing Officer was not correct in drawing any adverse inference against the assessee that no sale was made by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) had also taken into consideration that no material was brought on record to establish that the assessee had paid 3 per cent over and above the cheque amount received on account of sale of jewellery and diamonds. Therefore, the entire addition on account of sale of jewellery and also on account of commission at the rate of 3 per cent was deleted. The findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) were findings of fact, and they had not been controverted by the department. In addition to the facts discussed in the case of sale to ‘G’, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that ‘T’ had retracted from his earlier statement given during the course of investigation. In that way, additions made under sections 68 and 69C were deleted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in their entirety.

is the widening of the scope and the applicability of this anti-money laundering law. Now this law is applicable even to the gem and jewellery sector, which is predominantly cash dominated industry. The Amending Act has also introduced the concept of 'corresponding law' to link the provisions of the Indian law with the laws of the foreign countries. But these are not the only major amendments that have been made by the Amending Act. Some of the major amendments have been depicted in the following Table: 3. Impact of the amendments to the anti-money laundering law

3.1 Rules laid down by the Central Government - After gaining knowledge on the amendments to the India's anti-money laundering law, it becomes imperative to understand their impact on the concerned persons. For starters, all the requirements of reporting the details of prescribed transactions; maintenance of records of prescribed transactions; furnishing of prescribed information which was earlier applicable to banks, financial institutions, intermediaries shall now be applicable to all reporting entities. It's pertinent to mention here that in this regard, the Central Government has prescribed the Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records of the Nature and Value of Transactions, the Procedure and Manner of Maintaining and Time for Furnishing Information and Verification and Maintenance of Records of the Identity of the Clients of the Banking Companies, Financial Institutions and Intermediaries) Rules, 2005 ('the Rules' for short).

3.2 Rules prescribed under the Original Act would continue to operate - Like the original Act, even the Amending Act empowers the Central Government to prescribe the rules with respect to the maintenance of records, verification of the identity of client, furnishing of information, etc. Till now the Central Government has not prescribed any rules after the coming into force of the Amending Act. In such a case, it would be safe to presume that till the time any rules are prescribed under the Amended law, the Rules prescribed under the Original Act would continue to operate.

3.3 Mandatory maintenance and reporting of transactions by those covered under the law - As per the prescribed Rules, the maintenance and the reporting of the following transactions is mandatory by all those who are covered under the law:

all cash transactions of the value of more than rupees ten lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency;

all series of cash transactions integrally connected to each other which have been valued below rupees ten lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency, where such series of transactions have taken place within a month;

all transactions involving receipts by non-profit organisations of value more than rupees ten lakh, or its equivalent in foreign currency;

all cash transactions where forged or counterfeit currency notes or bank notes have been used as genuine or where any forgery of a valuable security or a document has taken place facilitating the transactions;

all suspicious transactions, whether or not made in cash.

These Rules have also prescribed the formats in which the reporting has to be done. Further, the time period within which such information has to be furnished has also been prescribed by these Rules.

3.4 Verification of the identity of the client - As far as the verification of the identity of the client is concerned, Rule 9 of the prescribed Rules prescribes that every banking company, financial institution and intermediary, as the case may be shall:

at the time of commencement of an account-based relationship, identify its clients, verify their identity and obtain information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship,

in all other cases, verify identity while carrying out the following:

transaction of an amount equal to or exceeding rupees fifty thousand, whether conducted as a single transaction or several transactions that appear to be connected, or

any international money transfer operations.

Conclusion

4. Considering the enormous amount of tainted money blocked in the Indian economy (especially in the real estate sector and gem & jewellery sector), the anti-money laundering law has been made applicable to these sectors. Objectively speaking, it was never a question of 'Will these sectors be covered or not?', rather it was always a case of 'When will these sectors be covered?'

The inclusion of the gem & jewellery sector under the ambit of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act has expectantly raised a large number of eyebrows among the multi-billion dollar jewellery industry in India. Their concerns are genuine. The issue is not whether these sectors should have been brought within its ambit or not, the problem lies in the lack of awareness among the dealers of precious metals and precious stones regarding their liability under this anti-money laundering law in India. On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

Restrictions under the Income Tax Act 1961 regarding cash transactions.

As per Section 269ST of the Income Tax Act 1961, no person shall receive an amount of two lakh rupees or more – (a) in aggregate from a person in a day; or (b) in respect of a single transaction; or (c) in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion from a person, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account.

Section 271DA of Income Tax Act, 1961, states that any person who receives an amount in violation of the terms and conditions of Section 269ST will be held liable to pay a penalty equivalent to the amount received in cash.

Therefore a combined reading of the provisions makes us perceive that the dealers in precious metals and/or stones will not normally engage in cash transactions with a customer for amount equal to or above Rupees ten lakhs.

In some of the cases, when old jewellery were given, they were taken for manufacturing new jewellery or to make certain customized changes required by customers. The view of the Assessing Officer that unless and until the sale and purchase were effected on same day, section 40A(3) was attracted cannot be accepted. [Para 12]

Applicability of rule 6DD of Income-tax Rules, 1962

• Thus, where the payments were effected to a customer on account of adjustment resulting out of an exchange of old jewellery with new jewellery, then it does get covered under the exception clause (d) of rule 6DD. [Para 13]

Violation of section 40A(3) in case of appearance of contra entries in cash book

• When in the cash book, assessee showed a purchase of jewellery for cash, the actual scenario was that it was only a credit purchase since there were contra entries in the cash book itself giving credit to concerned seller. At the time of effecting the sales, the entries were made in a reverse manner for adjusting against the credit. Such transactions could not be considered as violative of section 40A(3), just for a reason that contra entries appeared in the cash book. No doubt, assessee might have produced before Commissioner (Appeals) books of account, purchase vouchers and stock register. However, there is no violation of rule 46A for the reason that Assessing Officer has nowhere mentioned that assessee had failed to produce any records or books called for. Just because assessee could point out to Commissioner (Appeals), by producing the same cash book as produced before the Assessing Officer that there were no cash purchases whatsoever effected by it from its customers, will not be a reason to say that there was any violation of rule 46A. There is no case for the revenue that books produced by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) were different from the books produced by it before the Assessing Officer. [Para 13]

• In view of above, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the disallowance made under section 40A(3). [Para 15]

The immunity given by section 68 of the Finance Act, 1997 incorporating VDIS is limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery stands accepted and the amount credited in the books of the declarant to the extent of value of the jewellery so declared cannot be assessed as income of the declarant for any assessment year under any provision of the Income-tax Act including the provisions of section 68. This immunity, however, stops there and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further, either expressly or even by implication, to cover the sale of jewellery declared under VDIS also. The Assessing Officer is not only empowered to go into the genuineness of the transaction of sale of jewellery declared under VDIS, but he is duty-bound to do so in order to ensure that the scheme is not misused by the declarants for any more benefits than what are intended to be given under the scheme. It is, thus, open to the department to go into the genuineness of the transactions of sale of jewellery declared under VDIS and examine the same in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Income-tax Act. 11.11.5 Interest under section 206C(7)

Section 206C(7) provides for payment of simple interest in case of failure to collect whole or any part of tax, or after collecting payment thereof, by a person responsible for collecting tax.

Finance Act, 2012 inserts first proviso in section 206C(6A) (see para 11.8.4) to provide that in the circumstances specified therein the person shall not be deemed to be Assessee in default.

To charge the interest under sub-section (7) even in case of Assessee not deemed to be default, Finance Act, 2012 inserts a proviso in sub-section (7), effective 1-7-2012.

It provides that a person not deemed to be an assessee in default under the first proviso to sub-section (6A), who has failed to collect whole or any part of tax on any amount collected, would be liable to pay interest from the date on which the tax was collectible to the date of furnishing of return of income by a buyer etc.

To illustrate, the person was obliged to collect tax, say, on January 1. The buyer, etc., furnishes the return of income on July 31. The amount not collected by way of tax, say, is, say, Rs. 10,000. The person would be liable to pay interest on Rs. 10,000 for the period January 1 to July 31.

Commissioner (Appeals) that by way of the impugned proceedings, the Assessing Officer was making an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act . That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further. In the instant case, the department had examined four persons, who had declared jewellery under the VDIS and effected sale of such jewellery to the assessee-firm. The Assessing Officer had examined the genuineness of the business of purchase and sale of jewellery carried out by the concerned jeweller. There are no fetters on such powers of the Assessing Officer. The department was not hampered or impinged, by the immunity outlined in the VDIS to undertake such investigations. Hence, there was no justification in the stand of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the acceptance of the VDIS declarations by the Department in the hands of the sellers of the jewellery to the assessee made the impugned investigations contrary to the letter and spirit of the VDIS. Another important feature, which according to the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the case of the assessee was the registration of the assessee under the Punjab General Sales-tax Act, 1948. The crux of the dispute revolved around the purchase and sale of old diamond jewellery, which had been made only up to the period 17-3-1998. After 17-3-1998 and upto 31-3-1998, no such purchase or sale had been effected. The sales made up to 17-3-1998 had not been made a subject-matter of the sales tax returns submitted by the assessee, as admitted by the assessee. It was being sought to be explained on the ground that such sales were within the period of exemption and, hence, no sales tax was exigible on such sales. Be that as it may, the fact remained that such sales had not been subject to any verification/examination by the sales tax authorities too, for the same, being sales up to 17-3-1998, had not been reported in the sales tax return filed by the assessee. The reference made by the Commissioner (Appeals) to the assessee's sales tax assessment order, dated 4-12-2000, was also misplaced because that was in relation to the subsequent period, which was not relevant to the assessment year under consideration. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) erred in relying on the assessment order of the sales tax authority, dated 4-12-2000, for the subsequent period and the surrendering of sales tax registration certificate on 11-3-1999 to repeal the inference of the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the inference of the Assessing Officer that no actual business of purchase and sale was carried out by the assessee was justified and deserved to be upheld.

The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

an attempt to go behind the VDIS, was fallacious. The immunity given by section 68 of the VDIS, was limited to the extent that the existence of jewellery declared by a declarant stood accepted and the amount credited in the books of such declarant to the extent of value of jewellery so declared could not be assessed as income of such declarant for any assessment year under the Act. That immunity ends at the above stage and there is no provision in the scheme to extend the same further . In the instant case, the department had examined four persons, who had declared jewellery under the VDIS and effected sale of such jewellery to the assessee-firm. The Assessing Officer had examined the genuineness of the business of purchase and sale of jewellery carried out by the concerned jeweller. There are no fetters on such powers of the Assessing Officer. The department was not hampered or impinged, by the immunity outlined in the VDIS to undertake such investigations. Hence, there was no justification in the stand of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the acceptance of the VDIS declarations by the Department in the hands of the sellers of the jewellery to the assessee made the impugned investigations contrary to the letter and spirit of the VDIS. Another important feature, which according to the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the case of the assessee was the registration of the assessee under the Punjab General Sales-tax Act, 1948. The crux of the dispute revolved around the purchase and sale of old diamond jewellery, which had been made only up to the period 17-3-1998. After 17-3-1998 and upto 31-3-1998, no such purchase or sale had been effected. The sales made up to 17-3-1998 had not been made a subject-matter of the sales tax returns submitted by the assessee, as admitted by the assessee. It was being sought to be explained on the ground that such sales were within the period of exemption and, hence, no sales tax was exigible on such sales. Be that as it may, the fact remained that such sales had not been subject to any verification/examination by the sales tax authorities too, for the same, being sales up to 17-3-1998, had not been reported in the sales tax return filed by the assessee. The reference made by the Commissioner (Appeals) to the assessee's sales tax assessment order, dated 4-12-2000, was also misplaced because that was in relation to the subsequent period, which was not relevant to the assessment year under consideration. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) erred in relying on the assessment order of the sales tax authority, dated 4-12-2000, for the subsequent period and the surrendering of sales tax registration certificate on 11-3-1999 to repeal the inference of the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the inference of the Assessing Officer that no actual business of purchase and sale was carried out by the assessee was justified and deserved to be upheld.
